Constructing sampling schemes via coupling: Markov semigroups and optimal transport

N. Nüsken and G. A. Pavliotis
Abstract

In this paper we develop a general framework for constructing and analysing coupled Markov chain Monte Carlo samplers, allowing for both (possibly degenerate) diffusion and piecewise deterministic Markov processes. For many performance criteria of interest, including the asymptotic variance, the task of finding efficient couplings can be phrased in terms of problems related to optimal transport theory. We investigate general structural properties, proving a singularity theorem that has both geometric and probabilistic interpretations. Moreover, we show that those problems can often be solved approximately and support our findings with numerical experiments. For the particular objective of estimating the variance of a Bayesian posterior, our analysis suggests using novel techniques in the spirit of antithetic variates. Addressing the convergence to equilibrium of coupled processes we furthermore derive a modified Poincaré inequality.

1 Introduction and motivation

Many computational problems arising in machine learning, Bayesian statistics, molecular dynamics and various other fields require the approximation of probability distributions (in the following denoted by π\pi) on a high-dimensional space EE. In particular, uncertainty quantification in a Bayesian framework is intimately related to the evaluation of appropriate summary statistics such as the variance of the posterior [35, Chapter 10], [79, Chapter 8], [80, Chapter 6]. Often, this task is approached by considering empirical measures associated to an ensemble of nn particles, i.e. approximations of the form

π≈1n​∑i=1nδX(i)=:π~,\pi\approx\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta_{X^{(i)}}=:\tilde{\pi}, (1)

where X(i)X^{(i)} stands for the location of the iith particle and δx\delta_{x} denotes the Dirac measure centred at x∈Ex\in E. Usually, the particles are moved according to some (more often than not stochastic) dynamics, judiciously crafted in order for the empirical measure π~t:=1n​∑i=1nδXt(i)\tilde{\pi}_{t}:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta_{X_{t}^{(i)}} to approach π\pi when tt reaches a terminal value (finite or infinite). This methodology has been particularly influential in statistical inference of hidden-state Markov models (stochastic filtering or sequential Monte Carlo, see for instance [72], [25] and references therein). Ensemble based methods have also been employed in the contexts of optimisation [70, 73], molecular dynamics [77], Markov chain Monte Carlo [52, 64], or variational Bayesian inference [57]. Let us also mention the works [2] and [40], combining different aspects of various sampling strategies. The increasing availability of parallel-processing computational architectures has further encouraged the development and analysis of similar methodologies.

From an abstract perspective, many of the aforementioned algorithms targeting a probability measure π\pi on some state space EE naturally produce probability measures π¯\bar{\pi} on the product space E¯=∏i=1nEi\bar{E}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}E_{i}, where EiE_{i} is an identical copy of EE, standing for the state space of the iith particle. Denoting by Pi:𝒫⁡(E¯)→𝒫⁡(Ei)P_{i}:\mathcal{P}(\bar{E})\rightarrow\mathcal{P}(E_{i}) the mappings that send probability measures on E¯\bar{E} to their marginals on EiE_{i}, one then obtains the measure

1n​∑i=1nPi​(π¯)\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}P_{i}(\bar{\pi}) (2)

as an approximation for π\pi. Clearly, the map

Π:𝒫⁡(E¯)→𝒫⁡(E),π¯↦1n​∑i=1nPi​(π¯)\Pi:\mathcal{P}(\bar{E})\rightarrow\mathcal{P}(E),\quad\bar{\pi}\mapsto\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}P_{i}(\bar{\pi}) (3)

is far from injective since Π⁡(π¯)\Pi(\bar{\pi}) only depends on the marginals of π¯\bar{\pi}. This viewpoint shows that there is a considerable flexibility when generating the joint measure π¯\bar{\pi}, immediately suggesting fruitful connections to the theory of couplings of probability measures [56, 82] prominently encountered for instance in relation to optimal transport problems [84, 86] or decay estimates in Wasserstein distances (see for instance [30]). Since in applications Π⁡(π¯)\Pi(\bar{\pi}) is only an approximation of the target measure of interest, the freedom to design appropriate couplings can be used to suppress bias, variance and discretisation errors. This general idea has proved to be very versatile, leading to powerful simulation techniques such as multilevel Monte Carlo [36], coupling from the past [71] and antithetic variates [47, Section 9.2].

1.1 Couplings and Markov Chain Monte Carlo

In this paper we focus on coupling techniques in the context of Markov chain Monte Carlo simulations. Assume that we are interested in computing the expectation

𝔼π​f=∫Ef​𝑑π\mathbb{E}_{\pi}f=\int_{E}f\mathrm{d}\pi (4)

of a given test function (henceforth called observable) f:E→ℝf:E\rightarrow\mathbb{R} with respect to some probability measure π\pi on EE. As approximations relying on quadratures tend to be computationally infeasible in high dimensions, a standard approach is to construct a Markov process (Xt)t≥0(X_{t})_{t\geq 0} on EE such that

limT→∞1T​∫0Tf⁡(Xs)​𝑑s=∫Ef​𝑑π,\lim_{T\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}f(X_{s})\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_{E}f\mathrm{d}\pi, (5)

i.e. the process (Xt)t≥0(X_{t})_{t\geq 0} is supposed to be ergodic with respect to π\pi. More generally, one often constructs a Markov process (X¯t)t≥0(\bar{X}_{t})_{t\geq 0} on an extended state space E¯\bar{E}, ergodic with respect to a measure π¯\bar{\pi} that has π\pi as its marginal,

∫π¯​(x,y)​𝑑y=π​(x),\int\bar{\pi}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}y=\pi(x), (6)

where (x,y)∈E¯(x,y)\in\bar{E} and x∈Ex\in E. This idea is used for instance in Hamiltonian Monte Carlo [65] or sampling schemes based on underdamped Langevin dynamics [53, Chapter 2]. We also refer to the introduction in [28] for a more general perspective. In this work we take this approach further, in the sense that we consider extended measures π¯\bar{\pi} that have fixed marginals with respect to (multiple) complimentary subspaces of E¯\bar{E}. Immediately, this viewpoint suggests fruitful connections to theory of optimal (multimarginal) transportation.

To explain our approach, let us consider nn identical copies of EE, (Xt)t≥0(X_{t})_{t\geq 0} and π\pi, denoted by EiE_{i}, (Xti)t≥0(X^{i}_{t})_{t\geq 0} and πi\pi_{i}, for i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}. Our main object of study is the class of Markovian couplings (X¯t)t≥0(\bar{X}_{t})_{t\geq 0} of {(Xti)t≥0:i∈{1,…,n}}\left\{(X_{t}^{i})_{t\geq 0}:\,i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\right\} on the product space E¯=∏i=1nEi\bar{E}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}E_{i} that obey certain mild regularity assumptions. In particular, we characterise those couplings in terms of their infinitesimal generators in Section 2 (see Proposition 8). One of the recurring themes of this work is the use of the latter in the analysis of coupled processes. From the coupling property of (X¯t)t≥0(\bar{X}_{t})_{t\geq 0} it follows immediately that if this process is ergodic, then its invariant measure (denoted by π¯\bar{\pi}) is a coupling of the nn copies of π\pi.

For an observable f∈L1​(π)f\in L^{1}(\pi), we can define the extended observable F:E¯→ℝF:\bar{E}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} by

F⁡(x1,…,xn)=1n​∑i=1nf⁡(xi).F(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(x_{i}). (7)

From (5) it is then immediate that

limT→∞1T​∫0TF⁡(X¯t)​𝑑t=∫Ef​𝑑π,\lim_{T\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}F(\bar{X}_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t=\int_{E}f\,\mathrm{d}\pi, (8)

i.e. the coupled process (X¯t)t≥0(\bar{X}_{t})_{t\geq 0} in conjunction with the observable (7) provides a valid sampling scheme. Let us remark that the framework we develop in Section 2 accommodates the case when the spaces EiE_{i}, the processes (Xti)t≥0(X^{i}_{t})_{t\geq 0} and the measures πi\pi_{i} are not identical, allowing for considerable flexibility in the construction of coupled samplers.

The study of observables of the form (7) provides a compelling dual perspective on the ‘sum of marginals’ operator (3). Denoting by ℬb​(E)\mathcal{B}_{b}(E) the space of bounded measureable functions we can consider the ‘extension operator’

Π∗:ℬb​(E)→ℬb​(E¯),f↦1n​∑i=1nfi,\Pi^{*}:\mathcal{B}_{b}(E)\rightarrow\mathcal{B}_{b}(\bar{E}),\quad f\mapsto\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}, (9)

provided by (7). For π¯∈𝒫⁡(E¯)\bar{\pi}\in\mathcal{P}(\bar{E}) and f∈ℬb​(E)f\in\mathcal{B}_{b}(E) we clearly have (Π​π¯)​(f)=π¯​(Π∗​f)(\Pi\bar{\pi})(f)=\bar{\pi}(\Pi^{*}f), showing that understanding the class of observables given by (7) is sufficient for analysing the properties of measures of the form (2). This idea features in particular in Section 6 in the analysis of the exponential convergence to equilibrium for coupled processes.

Clearly, it is desirable to choose the coupling in such a way that the convergence in (8) is as fast as possible. Reasonable criteria involve the asymptotic variance (related to appropriate central limit theorems) and the spectral gap (related to the speed of convergence to equilbrium), both of which will be addressed in the present paper. We refer the reader to [28, Section 1] for a more detailed discussion of these quantities.

Similar constructions to ours have been considered in the literature, in particular in a discrete time setting. In [34], the authors construct coupled Gibbs samplers using a very related rationale (see also [41] and [63]). Coupled Metropolis-Hastings samplers have been put forward in [20]. The work [21] provides a theoretical framework that is however is quite different from the one developed in the present paper. Further algorithmic ideas related to coupled samplers can also be found in [50] and [75].

1.2 Overview of the main results by means of a simple example

In this section we present our main findings informally by means of a very simple example, pointing to the exact statements in the forthcoming sections. Let us stress that our results hold in much greater generality, in particular also including the recently fashionable piecewise deterministic Markov processes (PDMPs).

Let us consider n=2n=2 particles (the locations of which are denoted by XtX_{t} and YtY_{t}) moving each in one dimension according to the overdamped Langevin dynamics defined by the SDEs

d​Xt\displaystyle\mathrm{d}X_{t} =−V′​(Xt)​d​t+2​d​Btx,\displaystyle=-V^{\prime}(X_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}B^{x}_{t}, (10a)
d​Yt\displaystyle\mathrm{d}Y_{t} =−V′​(Yt)​d​t+2​d​Bty,\displaystyle=-V^{\prime}(Y_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}B^{y}_{t}, (10b)

where V∈C∞​(ℝ)V\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) is a fixed potential such that

Z:=∫ℝe−V​𝑑x<∞,Z:=\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-V}\mathrm{d}x<\infty, (11)

and (Btx)t≥0(B_{t}^{x})_{t\geq 0}, (Bty)t≥0(B_{t}^{y})_{t\geq 0} denote standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. As is well-known, each of these processes considered separately is ergodic with respect to π=1Z​e−V​d​x\pi=\frac{1}{Z}e^{-V}\mathrm{d}x, i.e. (5) holds for an appropriate class of observables. Note that we have deliberately refrained from stating that the Brownian motions (Btx)t≥0(B^{x}_{t})_{t\geq 0} and (Bty)t≥0(B^{y}_{t})_{t\geq 0} are independent. Indeed, notwithstanding any dependence between these, it is immediate that (8) holds for the extended observable F⁡(x,y)=12​(f⁡(x)+f⁡(y))F(x,y)=\frac{1}{2}(f(x)+f(y)), as defined in (7). One of the main objectives of our analysis is to find couplings between (Btx)t≥0(B^{x}_{t})_{t\geq 0} and (Bty)t≥0(B^{y}_{t})_{t\geq 0} such that the induced joint process (Xt,Yt)t≥0(X_{t},Y_{t})_{t\geq 0} has favourable properties, in terms of the asymptotic variance associated to (8) as well as in terms of convergence to equilibrium of Π⁡(π¯t)\Pi(\bar{\pi}_{t}), where π¯t\bar{\pi}_{t} denotes the joint law of (Xt,Yt)(X_{t},Y_{t}) and Π\Pi has been defined in (3). The dependence between (Btx)t≥0(B_{t}^{x})_{t\geq 0} and (Bty)t≥0(B_{t}^{y})_{t\geq 0} can be conveniently encoded in a suitable matrix-valued function G:ℝ2→ℝ2×2G:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}, writing

d​(XtYt)=(−V′​(Xt)−V′​(Yt))​d​t+2​G​(Xt,Yt)​(d​Wtxd​Wty),\mathrm{d}\begin{pmatrix}X_{t}\\ Y_{t}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-V^{\prime}(X_{t})\\ -V^{\prime}(Y_{t})\end{pmatrix}\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}G(X_{t},Y_{t})\begin{pmatrix}\mathrm{d}W_{t}^{x}\\ \mathrm{d}W_{t}^{y}\end{pmatrix}, (12)

for two independent Brownian motions (Wtx)t≥0(W_{t}^{x})_{t\geq 0} and (Wty)t≥0(W_{t}^{y})_{t\geq 0}. In this sense, the optimisation problem alluded to above is naturally posed over an appropriate set of matrix-valued functions.

In Section 2 we introduce the general framework, leading to a characterisation of possible couplings in terms of infinitesimal generators of the dynamics. In the present example, the generators of the one-particle dynamics are given by

ℒx=−V′(x)∂x+∂x2,ℒy=−V′(y)∂y+∂y2.\mathcal{L}_{x}=-V^{\prime}(x)\partial_{x}+\partial_{x}^{2},\quad\mathcal{L}_{y}=-V^{\prime}(y)\partial_{y}+\partial_{y}^{2}. (13)

The generators of possible couplings (Xt,Yt)t≥0(X_{t},Y_{t})_{t\geq 0} turn out to be of the form

ℒ¯Γ:=ℒx+ℒy+Γ,Γ=2α∂x∂y,\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}:=\mathcal{L}_{x}+\mathcal{L}_{y}+\Gamma,\quad\Gamma=2\alpha\partial_{x}\partial_{y}, (14)

where α:ℝ2→[−1,1]\alpha:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow[-1,1] is a function with suitable regularity properties. The connection between α\alpha and GG will be made precise in Section 3. We use the term ‘coupling operator’ when referring to Γ\Gamma and denote the set of such operators by 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Note that Γ\Gamma as defined in (14) vanishes on functions that depend either only on xx or only on yy. In Proposition 8 we will see that this property essentially characterises coupling operators in general. As it turns out (see the discussion in Section 2.3), not every coupling of ergodic Markov processes is such that the joint process is ergodic. Hence, we introduce the subset 𝒢0⊂𝒢\mathcal{G}^{0}\subset\mathcal{G} of ergodic coupling operators that do preserve ergodicity. In the present example, ℒ¯Γ\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma} is elliptic whenever −1<α<1-1<\alpha<1 pointwise and therefore the corresponding coupling operators are ergodic. Intuitively, the nonergodic coupling operators in 𝒢∖𝒢0\mathcal{G}\setminus\mathcal{G}^{0} can hence be thought of as lying ‘at the boundary’ of 𝒢0\mathcal{G}^{0}. Although we have not been successful in proving a rigorous version of this statement in a general context, the reader is encouraged to keep this picture in mind.

On 𝒢0\mathcal{G}^{0} we can consider the map Γ↦π¯Γ\Gamma\mapsto\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}, where π¯Γ\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma} stands for the unique invariant measure associated with ℒ¯Γ\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}. It is immediately clear from the construction that any π¯Γ\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma} arising in this way is a coupling of π\pi to itself (i.e. π¯Γ\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma} has marginal π\pi in both directions). We argue in Section 4 that a wide range of optimisation problems in our context can be cast in the following form, very closely linked to the theory of optimal transportation,

min⁡∫E¯Γ∈𝒢0⁡c​d​π¯Γ,\min_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}^{0}}\int_{\bar{E}}c\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}, (15)

where cc is an appropriate cost function. Indeed, we show in Section 4.1 that the task of optimising the asymptotic variance of a coupled process with respect to a given observable is equivalent to (15), for a cost function that is constructed from the solution of a related Poisson equation. Addressing the problem (15), we first note that the dependence Γ↦∫E¯c​d​π¯Γ\Gamma\mapsto\int_{\bar{E}}c\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma} is highly nonlinear, in particular, for Γ∈𝒢0\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}^{0} and λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1], the mapping λ↦∫E¯c​d​π¯λ​Γ\lambda\mapsto\int_{\bar{E}}c\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\lambda\Gamma} generally exhibits many local minima and maxima11 1 This claim is made assuming that λ​Γ∈𝒢0\lambda\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}^{0} for all λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1].. Nevertheless, we find that under suitable conditions the function Γ↦∫E¯c​d​π¯Γ\Gamma\mapsto\int_{\bar{E}}c\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma} does not attain its extrema on interior points. This is the main result of Section 4.2 and is stated rigorously in Theorem 47. In the example under consideration, this implies that optimal couplings necessarily satisfy ‖α‖∞=1\|\alpha\|_{\infty}=1, leading to singular (i.e. degenerately elliptic) generators ℒ¯Γ\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}. This conclusion is interesting in two respects: Firstly, it complements standard results from optimal transport theory showing that optimal couplings are typically singular in a certain sense. We stress, however, that the problem (15) is genuinely different from problems occurring in optimal transport theory, and that our proof uses fundamentally different techniques. Secondly, this result supports the folklore that optimal MCMC samplers use the least amount of noise necessary to guarantee their ergodicity.

While the results from Section 4 indicate the possible locations of optimal coupling operators Γ\Gamma in the set 𝒢\mathcal{G}, they do not help to actually find them in practice. In Section 5 we address this problem by considering small perturbations around the trivial coupling 𝟎∈𝒢\mathbf{0}\in\mathcal{G} corresponding to independent Brownian motions. This leads to a much more tractable optimisation problem that can be solved explicitly in concrete examples and gives promising results in our numerical experiments. In the present example, ‘mirror coupling’ (Btx=−BtyB_{t}^{x}=-B_{t}^{y}) turns out to be optimal in terms of reducing the asymptotic variance of monotone observables, in the sense of the optimisation problem just referred to. However, for different observables (perhaps exhibiting other types of symmetries) more intricate coupling strategies turn out to be advisable. We wish to stress that those observables are of particular relevance for the quantification of uncertainty in a Bayesian framework, for instance in the computation of the variance or related quantities of a posterior distribution.

In Section 6 we analyse the rate of convergence to equilibrium for coupled processes. As we will see, the former can be characterised in terms of an inequality of Poincaré type that is in turn related to an appropriate Hilbert space constructed in terms of the coupling. Applied to the present example, this result shows that the rate of convergence can be improved relative to the one-particle dynamics if the potential VV is symmetric, i.e. V⁡(x)=V⁡(−x)V(x)=V(-x). In general, the speed of convergence to equilibrium can also be slower, in the sense that there might appear a constant C>1C>1 in front of the exponential decay estimate. We leave a more detailed exploration of this phenomenon for future study.

The structure of the paper is as follows: In Section 2, we introduce our framework in a general setting. In particular, we fix the notation (Section 2.1), characterise coupled processes in terms of their generators (Section 2.2), discuss ergodic properties (Section 2.3) and provide a means of construction coupling operators given the generators of the marginal processes (Section 2.4). In Section 3, we illustrate our theory with concrete examples, namely diffusion processes overdamped Langevin dynamics (Section 3.1), underdamped Langevin dynamics (Section 3.2), as well as the zigzag process (Section 3.3), representing the class of piecewise deterministic Markov processes. In Section 4.1 we derive a central theorem for coupled processes. The ensuing expression for the asymptotic variance is connected to the theory of optimal transportation, as exhibited and analysed in Section 4.2. In Section 5 we take a perturbative approach towards the solutions of the aforementioned optimal transport problems and exemplify our results in the context of the examples presented in Section 3. Finally, in Section 6 we analyse the convergence of coupled processes to equilibrium relying on a suitable functional inequality of Poincaré type. The appendix comprises additional material required for some of the proofs throughout the article.

2 Coupled processes and coupling operators

This section is devoted to the interplay between couplings of Markov processes and their infinitesimal generators. We start by specifying the setting and notations.

2.1 Preliminaries, notation and setting

2.1.1 Feller semigroups

For a given locally compact Polish space EE we will denote the space of bounded, Borel measurable functions by ℬb​(E)\mathcal{B}_{b}(E), the space of bounded continuous functions by Cb​(E)C_{b}(E), and the space of continuous functions vanishing at infinity22 2 Recall that a function f:Ei→ℝf:E_{i}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} vanishes at infinity if for all ε>0\varepsilon>0 there exists a compact set K⊂EiK\subset E_{i} such that |f⁡(x)|≤ε|f(x)|\leq\varepsilon for all x∈Ei∖Kx\in E_{i}\setminus K. by C0​(E)C_{0}(E). The space of probability measures on EE (equipped with the Borel σ\sigma-algebra ℬ⁡(E)\mathcal{B}(E)) will be denoted by 𝒫⁡(E)\mathcal{P}(E). All of theses spaces become Banach spaces when equipped with the supremum norm, denoted by ∥⋅∥∞\|\cdot\|_{\infty}. An EE-valued Markov process (Xt)t≥0(X_{t})_{t\geq 0} induces a semigroup of linear operators (St)t≥0(S_{t})_{t\geq 0} on ℬb​(E)\mathcal{B}_{b}(E) via

(St​f)​(x)=𝔼⁡[f⁡(Xt)|X0=x],f∈ℬb​(E),x∈E.(S_{t}f)(x)=\mathbb{E}[f(X_{t})|X_{0}=x],\quad f\in\mathcal{B}_{b}(E),\,x\in E. (16)

Since the terminology varies slightly across the literature, we next give the definition of Feller processes used in this paper, mostly adopting the notations and conventions from [13, Chapter 1]. For more details we furthermore refer to [44, Chapter 17].

Definition 1 (Feller processes).

A Markov process (Xt)t≥0(X_{t})_{t\geq 0} satisfies the Feller property if the following hold for the corresponding semigroup (St)t≥0(S_{t})_{t\geq 0}:

  1. 1.

    (St)t≥0(S_{t})_{t\geq 0} leaves C0​(E)C_{0}(E) invariant, i.e. St​f∈C0​(E)S_{t}f\in C_{0}(E) for all f∈C0​(E)f\in C_{0}(E) and t≥0t\geq 0.

  2. 2.

    (St)t≥0(S_{t})_{t\geq 0} is strongly continuous on C0​(E)C_{0}(E), i.e.

    ‖St​f−f‖∞→t→00\|S_{t}f-f\|_{\infty}\xrightarrow{t\rightarrow 0}0 (17)

    for all f∈C0​(E)f\in C_{0}(E).

Provided that (St)t≥0(S_{t})_{t\geq 0} is a Feller semigroup as specified above, we define its generator (ℒ,𝒟⁡(ℒ))(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{L})) in the usual way [31][Chapter 2]. Throughout this paper, we will assume for convenience that the state space EE has a differential structure such that the space Cc∞​(E)C_{c}^{\infty}(E) of compactly supported smooth functions is meaningfully defined. We can then make the following assumption on the domain of the generator ℒ\mathcal{L}:

Assumption 1.

All considered Feller processes are rich33 3 We adopt this terminology following for instance [48, Section 1.5] and references therein., i.e. Cc∞​(E)⊂𝒟⁡(ℒ)C_{c}^{\infty}(E)\subset\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{L}).

The state spaces encountered in the examples in Section 3 naturally admit differentiable structures and the corresponding generators fulfil Assumption 1. Let us remark, however, that our framework can be extended to more general scenarios (including for instance infinite dimensional examples), replacing Cc∞​(E)C_{c}^{\infty}(E) by suitable function spaces adapted to the particular setting.

Remark 2.

Clearly, C0​(E)C_{0}(E) does not contain constant functions (apart from the zero function) if EE is not compact. In preparation for Definition 6, we mention that 𝒟⁡(ℒ)\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{L}) can naturally be extended to a subset of Cb​(E)C_{b}(E) by endowing the latter with the topology of uniform convergence on compact subsets of EE. Following [78] (see also [43, Section 4.8]), the extended generator (ℒ~,𝒟⁡(ℒ~))(\tilde{\mathcal{L}},\mathcal{D}(\tilde{\mathcal{L}})) can then be defined by

𝒟⁡(ℒ~)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}(\tilde{\mathcal{L}}) ={f∈Cb(E):limt→0St​f−ftexists uniformly on compact sets},\displaystyle=\left\{f\in C_{b}(E):\,\lim_{t\rightarrow 0}\frac{S_{t}f-f}{t}\quad\text{exists uniformly on compact sets}\right\}, (18a)
ℒ~​f\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{L}}f =limt→0St​f−ft,f∈𝒟⁡(ℒ~).\displaystyle=\lim_{t\rightarrow 0}\frac{S_{t}f-f}{t},\quad f\in\mathcal{D}(\tilde{\mathcal{L}}). (18b)

Since (St)t≥0(S_{t})_{t\geq 0} is conservative44 4 Conservativeness of the semigroup (St)t≥0(S_{t})_{t\geq 0} means that S1​𝟏=𝟏S_{1}\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1} for all t≥0t\geq 0, encoding the conservation of total probability mass. we immediately see that 𝟏∈𝒟⁡(ℒ~)\mathbf{1}\in\mathcal{D}(\tilde{\mathcal{L}}) and ℒ~​𝟏=0\tilde{\mathcal{L}}\mathbf{1}=0, i.e. ℒ~\tilde{\mathcal{L}} vanishes on constant functions. Moreover, (ℒ~,𝒟⁡(ℒ~))(\tilde{\mathcal{L}},\mathcal{D}(\tilde{\mathcal{L}})) is an extension of (ℒ,𝒟⁡(ℒ))(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{L})), i.e. 𝒟⁡(ℒ)⊂𝒟⁡(ℒ~)\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{L})\subset\mathcal{D}(\tilde{\mathcal{L}}) and ℒ~|𝒟⁡(ℒ)=ℒ\tilde{\mathcal{L}}|_{\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{L})}=\mathcal{L}. Henceforth we will thus drop the tilde when no confusion is possible.

2.1.2 Product spaces

We will be dealing with a collection of locally compact Polish spaces EiE_{i}, indexed by i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, and denote their cartesian product by E¯:=E1×…×En\bar{E}:=E_{1}\times\ldots\times E_{n}. For f∈ℬb​(Ei)f\in\mathcal{B}_{b}(E_{i}), it is of course understood that also f∈ℬb​(E¯)f\in\mathcal{B}_{b}(\bar{E}), then depending only on the coordinate xix_{i} in x¯≡(x1,…,xn)\bar{x}\equiv(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}). To a given function f∈Cc∞​(Ei)f\in C_{c}^{\infty}(E_{i}) or f∈C0​(Ei)f\in C_{0}(E_{i}), we will also associate the canonical element in ℬb​(E¯)\mathcal{B}_{b}(\bar{E}), but wish to emphasize that clearly ff does not in general have compact support or does not vanish at infinity when considered as a function on E¯\bar{E}. Frequently, the spaces EiE_{i} will be identical copies of each other, i.e. E¯=En\bar{E}=E^{n}. Given f∈ℬb​(E)f\in\mathcal{B}_{b}(E), we will then write fi∈ℬb​(E¯)f_{i}\in\mathcal{B}_{b}(\bar{E}) for the function given by

fi​(x1,…,xn)=f⁡(xi),(x1,…,xn)∈E¯.f_{i}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=f(x_{i}),\quad(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\bar{E}. (19)

Sums of unbounded operators are defined in the usual way: For two operators (A,𝒟⁡(A))(A,\mathcal{D}(A)) and (B,𝒟⁡(B))(B,\mathcal{D}(B)) defined on the same Banach space XX (i.e. 𝒟⁡(A)⊂X\mathcal{D}(A)\subset X and 𝒟⁡(B)⊂X\mathcal{D}(B)\subset X), their sum is defined via

(A+B)​f:=A​f+B​f,f∈𝒟⁡(A+B):=𝒟⁡(A)∩𝒟⁡(B),(A+B)f:=Af+Bf,\quad f\in\mathcal{D}(A+B):=\mathcal{D}(A)\cap\mathcal{D}(B), (20)

see for instance [31, Chapter III]. In the case when (A,𝒟⁡(A))(A,\mathcal{D}(A)) and (B,𝒟⁡(B))(B,\mathcal{D}(B)) are defined on two distinct spaces ℬb​(Ei)\mathcal{B}_{b}(E_{i}) and ℬb​(Ej)\mathcal{B}_{b}(E_{j}), i≠ji\neq j, (i.e. 𝒟⁡(A)⊂ℬb​(Ei)\mathcal{D}(A)\subset\mathcal{B}_{b}(E_{i}) and 𝒟⁡(B)⊂ℬb​(Ej)\mathcal{D}(B)\subset\mathcal{B}_{b}(E_{j})), their sum is defined as

A+B:=A⊗I+I⊗B,𝒟⁡(A+B):=𝒟⁡(A)​⊗^​𝒟​(B),A+B:=A\otimes I+I\otimes B,\quad\mathcal{D}(A+B):=\mathcal{D}(A)\widehat{\otimes}\mathcal{D}(B), (21)

where ⊗^\widehat{\otimes} denotes the canonical topological tensor product on ℬb​(Ei×Ej)\mathcal{B}_{b}(E_{i}\times E_{j}) (see [1] and [4, A-I 3.7]).

2.2 Coupled processes

Assume that for i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, we are given locally compact Polish spaces EiE_{i}, representing the state spaces of nn distinct particles. Furthermore, for i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, let us fix Feller semigroups (Sti)t≥0(S^{i}_{t})_{t\geq 0} on EiE_{i} with generators (ℒi,𝒟⁡(ℒi))(\mathcal{L}_{i},\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{L}_{i})) and associated Feller processes (Xti)t≥0(X^{i}_{t})_{t\geq 0} on appropriate stochastic bases (Ωi,ℙi,(ℱti)t≥0)(\Omega_{i},\mathbb{P}_{i},(\mathcal{F}^{i}_{t})_{t\geq 0}), representing the dynamics of those particles (in the following these processes will be referred to as the ‘one-particle dynamics’). Let us also assume that the spaces Cc∞​(Ei)C_{c}^{\infty}(E_{i}) are cores for the semigroups (Sti)t≥0(S_{t}^{i})_{t\geq 0}.

Remark 3.

By Watanabe’s Theorem (see for instance [44, Proposition 17.9]), Cc∞​(Ei)C_{c}^{\infty}(E_{i}) is a core for ℒi\mathcal{L}_{i} if it is dense in 𝒟⁡(ℒi)\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{L}_{i}) and invariant under (Sti)t≥0(S^{i}_{t})_{t\geq 0}. It is possible to extend our framework by exchanging Cc∞​(Ei)C_{c}^{\infty}(E_{i}) for other cores, say 𝒟i\mathcal{D}_{i}, as long as the first condition in Defintion 6 is altered accordingly.

Consider now a Feller process (X¯t)t≥0(\bar{X}_{t})_{t\geq 0} on the product space E¯:=E1×…×En\bar{E}:=E_{1}\times\ldots\times E_{n}, together with its associated semigroup (S¯t)t≥0(\bar{S}_{t})_{t\geq 0} on ℬb​(E¯)\mathcal{B}_{b}(\bar{E}) and generator (ℒ¯,𝒟⁡(ℒ¯))(\bar{\mathcal{L}},\mathcal{D}(\bar{\mathcal{L}})) in C0​(E¯)C_{0}(\bar{E}). We will denote the EiE_{i}-valued coordinate processes of (X¯t)t≥0(\bar{X}_{t})_{t\geq 0} by (X¯ti)t≥0(\bar{X}_{t}^{i})_{t\geq 0}.

Definition 4 (Feller couplings).

The process (X¯t)t≥0(\bar{X}_{t})_{t\geq 0} is called a Feller coupling of the processes (Xti)t≥0(X^{i}_{t})_{t\geq 0}, if its marginals are given by these processes, i.e. if for all i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, the processes (X¯ti)t≥0(\bar{X}^{i}_{t})_{t\geq 0} and (Xti)t≥0(X_{t}^{i})_{t\geq 0} induce the same law on the space of càdlàg functions D⁡([0,∞),Ei)D([0,\infty),E_{i}) 55 5 Every Feller process has a càdlàg modification, see [13, Theorem 1.19]..

Our aim in this section is to characterise the infinitesimal generators of such coupled processes.

Remark 5.

We are making the following two assumptions when considering the class of processes described above. Firstly, we assume certain continuity properties of the process (X¯t)t≥0(\bar{X}_{t})_{t\geq 0}, encoded mainly in the fact that the space C0​(E¯)C_{0}(\bar{E}) is invariant under the action of the corresponding semigroup (see for instance [13, Lemma 1.4] for more details). Restricting our attention to the class of Feller processes allows us to use the theory of strongly continuous semigroups on Banach spaces [31] for the development of the theory in this section. In examples and applications however (see Sections 3 and 5), we will relax this assumption a bit, allowing for more general processes.

Secondly, we consider processes (X¯t)t≥0(\bar{X}_{t})_{t\geq 0} that are Markovian. Obviously there are many non-Markovian couplings of the underlying processes (Xti)t≥0(X_{t}^{i})_{t\geq 0} and indeed those might be of particular interest for applications. Hence we plan to investigate the possibility of extending our framework in this direction in a forthcoming project.

We now proceed to introduce a class of linear (unbounded) operators (Γ,𝒟⁡(Γ))(\Gamma,\mathcal{D}(\Gamma)) on ℬb​(E¯)\mathcal{B}_{b}(\bar{E}):

Definition 6 (Coupling operators).

Let (Γ,𝒟⁡(Γ))(\Gamma,\mathcal{D}(\Gamma)) be a (possibly unbounded) linear operator on ℬ⁡(E¯)\mathcal{B}(\bar{E}). Then (Γ,𝒟⁡(Γ))(\Gamma,\mathcal{D}(\Gamma)) is called a coupling operator if the following conditions are satisfied:

  1. 1.

    Test functions that depend on only one component of x¯=(x1,…,xn)\bar{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) are in the kernel of Γ\Gamma:

    For all i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\} and f∈Cc∞​(Ei)f\in C_{c}^{\infty}(E_{i}) it holds that f∈𝒟⁡(Γ)f\in\mathcal{D}(\Gamma) and

    Γ​f=0.\Gamma f=0. (22)
  2. 2.

    The operator

    ℒ¯Γ:=∑i=1nℒi+Γ\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}_{i}+\Gamma (23)

    with domain 𝒟⁡(ℒ¯Γ)=⨂i=1n𝒟⁡(ℒi)∩𝒟⁡(Γ)\mathcal{D}(\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma})=\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{L}_{i})\cap\mathcal{D}(\Gamma) is closable and its closure is the infinitesimal generator of a Feller process on E¯\bar{E}.

The Feller semigroup corresponding to a coupling operator Γ\Gamma will be referred to by (S¯tΓ)t≥0(\bar{S}_{t}^{\Gamma})_{t\geq 0}. Furthermore, the set of coupling operators will be denoted by 𝒢\mathcal{G}, i.e.

𝒢={Γ:𝒟(Γ)⊂ℬb(E¯)→ℬb(E¯):Conditions 1 and 2 are satisfied.}.\mathcal{G}=\{\Gamma:\mathcal{D}(\Gamma)\subset\mathcal{B}_{b}(\bar{E})\rightarrow\mathcal{B}_{b}(\bar{E}):\,\text{Conditions \ref{it:kernel} and \ref{it:generator} are satisfied.}\}.
Remark 7.

We will not distinguish (notationally) between ℒ¯Γ\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma} and its closure. Notice also that the first condition in Definition 6 necessitates to think of Γ\Gamma as an operator defined on (a subspace) of Cb​(E¯)C_{b}(\bar{E}) (rather than C0​(E¯)C_{0}(\bar{E})), because of Cc∞​(Ei)⊄C0​(E¯)C_{c}^{\infty}(E_{i})\not\subset C_{0}(\bar{E}). The second condition is naturally concerned with ℒ¯Γ\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma} being the generator of a semigroup on C0​(E¯)C_{0}(\bar{E}) (and hence with the appropriate restriction of Γ\Gamma). We refer to Remark 2 for a discussion about the extended generator on Cb​(E¯)C_{b}(\bar{E}).

We have the following result, characterising completely the set of rich Feller couplings in terms of the coupling operators 𝒢\mathcal{G}:

Proposition 8.

For any Γ∈𝒢\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}, the Feller process generated by ℒ¯Γ\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma} as defined in (23) is a coupling of the processes ((Xti)t≥0,i∈{1,…​n})\left((X^{i}_{t})_{t\geq 0},\,i\in\{1,\ldots n\}\right). Conversely, if (X¯t)t≥0(\bar{X}_{t})_{t\geq 0} is a Feller coupling of the processes ((Xti)t≥0,i∈{1,…​n})\left((X^{i}_{t})_{t\geq 0},\,i\in\{1,\ldots n\}\right), then its generator is of the form (23), with Γ∈𝒢\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}.

Proof.

Let Γ∈𝒢\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}, and consider the process (X¯t)t≥0(\bar{X}_{t})_{t\geq 0} generated by the corresponding operator ℒ¯Γ\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma} as defined in (23). Let us fix i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}. Clearly, Cc∞​(Ei)∈𝒟⁡(ℒ¯Γ)C_{c}^{\infty}(E_{i})\in\mathcal{D}(\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}) and ℒ¯Γ​f=ℒi​f\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}f=\mathcal{L}_{i}f for f∈Cc∞​(Ei)f\in C^{\infty}_{c}(E_{i}). Hence, for all f∈Cc∞​(Ei)f\in C_{c}^{\infty}(E_{i}), the process

f⁡(X¯t)−f⁡(X¯0)−∫0t(ℒi​f)​(X¯s)​𝑑s,t≥0,f(\bar{X}_{t})-f(\bar{X}_{0})-\int_{0}^{t}(\mathcal{L}_{i}f)(\bar{X}_{s})\,\mathrm{d}s,\quad t\geq 0, (24)

is a martingale with respect to the natural filtration (ℱtX¯)t≥0(\mathcal{F}^{\bar{X}}_{t})_{t\geq 0} generated by (X¯t)t≥0(\bar{X}_{t})_{t\geq 0}. From the uniqueness of the martingale problem for the generator ℒi\mathcal{L}_{i} (see for instance [32, Section 4.4]) and the fact that Cc∞​(Ei)C_{c}^{\infty}(E_{i}) is a core for ℒi\mathcal{L}_{i}, it follows that (X¯ti)t≥0(\bar{X}^{i}_{t})_{t\geq 0} has indeed the same law as (Xti)t≥0(X^{i}_{t})_{t\geq 0}.

Conversely, assume that (X¯t)t≥0(\bar{X}_{t})_{t\geq 0} is a Feller coupling of the processes ((Xti)t≥0,i∈{1,…​n})\left((X^{i}_{t})_{t\geq 0},\,i\in\{1,\ldots n\}\right) and denote its generator by (ℒ~,𝒟⁡(ℒ~))(\tilde{\mathcal{L}},\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{\tilde{L}})). For fixed i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, we first argue that Cc∞​(Ei)⊂𝒟⁡(ℒ~)C^{\infty}_{c}(E_{i})\subset\mathcal{D}(\tilde{\mathcal{L}}), referring to the domain of the extended generator defined in (18a). Indeed, this amounts to showing that for all f∈Cc∞​(Ei)f\in C_{c}^{\infty}(E_{i}) the limit

limt→01t​(S~t​f−f)\lim_{t\rightarrow 0}\frac{1}{t}(\tilde{S}_{t}f-f) (25)

exists uniformly on compact sets. By the coupling property (Definition 4), we have that S~t​f=Sti​f\tilde{S}_{t}f=S_{t}^{i}f for f∈Cc∞​(Ei)f\in C_{c}^{\infty}(E_{i}). Therefore (and since Cc∞​(Ei)⊂𝒟⁡(ℒi)C_{c}^{\infty}(E_{i})\subset\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{L}_{i}) by assumption), it follows that the limit (25) even exists uniformly on the whole of E¯\bar{E}.

We can now define Γ~:=ℒ~−∑i=1nℒi\tilde{\Gamma}:=\tilde{\mathcal{L}}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}_{i} on 𝒟⁡(Γ~):=𝒟⁡(ℒ~)∩⨂i=1n𝒟⁡(ℒi)\mathcal{D}(\tilde{\Gamma}):=\mathcal{D}(\tilde{\mathcal{L}})\cap\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{L}_{i}). It is then sufficient to show that Γ\Gamma satisfies the first condition of Definition 6. To this end, take f∈Cc∞​(Ei)f\in C_{c}^{\infty}(E_{i}) in the martingale problem for ℒ~\tilde{\mathcal{L}} to see that

f⁡(X¯ti)−f⁡(X¯0i)−∫0t(ℒi​f)​(X¯si)​𝑑s−∫0t(Γ~​f)​(X¯s)​𝑑s,t≥0,f(\bar{X}^{i}_{t})-f(\bar{X}^{i}_{0})-\int_{0}^{t}(\mathcal{L}_{i}f)(\bar{X}^{i}_{s})\,\mathrm{d}s-\int_{0}^{t}(\tilde{\Gamma}f)(\bar{X}_{s})\,\mathrm{d}s,\quad t\geq 0, (26)

is a martingale, again with respect to the natural filtration (ℱtX¯)t≥0(\mathcal{F}^{\bar{X}}_{t})_{t\geq 0} generated by (X¯t)t≥0(\bar{X}_{t})_{t\geq 0}. Since (X¯ti)t≥0(\bar{X}_{t}^{i})_{t\geq 0} and (Xti)t≥0(X_{t}^{i})_{t\geq 0} are equal in law by assumption, it follows that ((X¯ti)t≥0,(ℱtX¯)t≥0)((\bar{X}^{i}_{t})_{t\geq 0},(\mathcal{F}^{\bar{X}}_{t})_{t\geq 0}) is a solution to the martingale problem for ℒi\mathcal{L}_{i}. Hence, ∫0t(Γ~​f)​(X¯s)​𝑑s\int_{0}^{t}(\tilde{\Gamma}f)(\bar{X}_{s})\mathrm{d}s has to be a martingale as well. Remark 9.

Similar approaches, describing couplings in terms of coupling operators, are known from the literature. See for instance [17, Chapter 2, Definition 2.7] and references therein. The exact result of Proposition 8 and its proof using martingale problems seems to be new and in particular relevant for Conjecture 2.18 and Open Problem 2.19 in [17].

Example 10.

Independent (or trivial) coupling: The zero operator Γ=𝟎\Gamma=\mathbf{0} is always in 𝒢\mathcal{G}, as the conditions of Definition 6 clearly hold. Indeed, consider the operator

ℒ¯0:=∑i=1nℒi\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}_{i} (27)

on the domain 𝒟⁡(ℒ¯0):=⨁^i​𝒟​(ℒi)\mathcal{D}(\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}):=\widehat{\bigoplus}_{i}\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{L}_{i}). It is straightforward (see for instance [4, A-I 3.7]) to show that ℒ¯0\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0} is the generator of a Feller semigroup (S¯t0)t≥0(\bar{S}^{0}_{t})_{t\geq 0} given by

S¯t0​f=(∏i=1nSti)​f,f∈ℬb​(E¯),t≥0,\bar{S}^{0}_{t}f=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}S^{i}_{t}\right)f,\quad f\in\mathcal{B}_{b}(\bar{E}),\,t\geq 0, (28)

and that the associated Feller process is just (X¯t0)t≥0=(Xt1,…,Xtn)t≥0(\bar{X}^{0}_{t})_{t\geq 0}=(X_{t}^{1},\ldots,X_{t}^{n})_{t\geq 0}, i.e. it is obtained from independent copies of the underlying processes.

Let us briefly discuss some of the implications of the conditions in Definition 6. As can be seen from the proof of Proposition 8, the first condition is instrumental in guaranteeing that the coupled process (X¯t)t≥0(\bar{X}_{t})_{t\geq 0} has the correct marginals. To put the second condition into context, we remark that generators of Feller semigroups can be characterised by means of the Hille-Yosida-Ray theorem in terms of the positive maximum principle (see [13, Lemma 1.28] and [13, Theorem 1.30]). As we will see in Examples (Section 3), the latter often restricts the ‘size’ of coupling operators, so that the set 𝒢\mathcal{G} usually turns out to be ‘bounded’ in a certain sense. Let us close this section by mentioning the following conjecture:

Conjecture 11.

The set 𝒢\mathcal{G} is convex.

Resolving the above conjecture would shed further light on the structure of 𝒢\mathcal{G}, especially in connection with the results obtained in Section 4.

2.3 Ergodicity and regularity of couplings

From here on, let us make the following assumption, natural in the context of MCMC samplers:

Assumption 2.

The underlying one-particle processes (Xti)t≥0(X^{i}_{t})_{t\geq 0} are ergodic, i.e. for every i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\} there exists a unique probability measure πi∈𝒫⁡(Ei)\pi_{i}\in\mathcal{P}(E_{i}) on EiE_{i} such that

∫Ei(ℒi​f)​d​πi=0,f∈𝒟⁡(ℒi),\int_{E_{i}}(\mathcal{L}_{i}f)\,\mathrm{d}\pi_{i}=0,\quad f\in\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{L}_{i}), (29)

and, furthermore,

limT→∞1T​∫0Tf⁡(Xti)​𝑑t=∫Eif​d​πi,f∈Cb​(Ei).\lim_{T\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}f(X_{t}^{i})\,\mathrm{d}t=\int_{E_{i}}f\,\mathrm{d}\pi_{i},\quad f\in C_{b}(E_{i}). (30)

Following up on Example (10), we see that the semigroup (S¯t0)t≥0(\bar{S}^{0}_{t})_{t\geq 0} as given in (28) with generator ℒ¯0\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0} as defined in (27) is ergodic with respect to the product measure

π¯0:=⨂i=1nπi\bar{\pi}_{0}:=\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n}\pi_{i} (31)

on E¯\bar{E}. Unfortunately, it turns out that not all coupling operators Γ∈𝒢\Gamma\in\mathcal{G} induce ergodic coupled processes, even under the Assumption 2 (for an example, see [55, Section 3.1]). We therefore make the following definition:

Definition 12.

Ergodic couplings: A coupling operator Γ∈𝒢\Gamma\in\mathcal{G} is called ergodic, if the Feller process generated by ℒ¯Γ\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma} is ergodic. The corresponding subset of ergodic coupling operators will be denoted by 𝒢0\mathcal{G}^{0}. The unique invariant measure associated to Γ∈𝒢0\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}^{0} will be denoted by π¯Γ\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}.

Remark 13.

By construction, the measures π¯Γ\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma} are couplings of the one-particle invariant measures (πi)i=1n(\pi_{i})_{i=1}^{n}.

Remark 14.

For the analysis, ergodicity of the coupling is a crucial requirement (although with more work it might be possible to extend some of the results to the case when ergodicity fails to hold). Let us emphasize however that the validity of (8) does not depend on this, as only the marginal property of the coupling is used in its derivation. Hence in practice it is harmless to use nonergodic couplings, and in fact our results obtained in Section 4 (in particular, Theorem 47) suggest using couplings that are at least not straightforwardly seen to be ergodic. In this case, quantities measuring the performance of the sampler (such as the asymptotic variance corresponding to certain observables) might be undefined or depend on the initial condition.

In general, ergodicity might fail in various ways. For instance, the process might not admit any invariant measure at all, or convergence of ergodic averages (in the sense of (30)) might not hold. The following result shows that the situation is simpler in our context.

Lemma 15.

Let Assumption 2 be satisfied. Then the following hold:

  1. 1.

    Every Feller coupling admits at least one invariant measure.

  2. 2.

    If a Feller coupling admits a unique invariant measure, then the process is ergodic, i.e. (30) holds.

Proof.

We proceed along the lines of the proof of the Krylov-Bogolyubov theorem [22, Section 3.1]. Let νi∈𝒫⁡(Ei)\nu_{i}\in\mathcal{P}(E_{i}) be arbitrary initial conditions for the processes (Xti)t≥0(X_{t}^{i})_{t\geq 0}. By ergodicity, the families (π~ti)t≥0(\tilde{\pi}^{i}_{t})_{t\geq 0} of Césaro averages

π~ti​(A)=1t​∫0t((Ssi)∗​νi)​(A)​𝑑s,A∈ℬ⁡(Ei),\tilde{\pi}^{i}_{t}(A)=\frac{1}{t}\int_{0}^{t}\left((S_{s}^{i})^{*}\nu_{i}\right)(A)\,\mathrm{d}s,\quad A\in\mathcal{B}(E_{i}),

are convergent, and therefore tight. Let (X¯t)t≥0(\bar{X}_{t})_{t\geq 0} be a Feller coupling and denote the corresponding Césaro averages by (π¯~t)t≥0(\tilde{\bar{\pi}}_{t})_{t\geq 0}. For any t≥0t\geq 0, π¯~t\tilde{\bar{\pi}}_{t} is a coupling of (π~ti)i=1n(\tilde{\pi}^{i}_{t})_{i=1}^{n}. Using an obvious extension of [86, Lemma 4.4] to the multimarginal case, we see that (π¯~t)t≥0(\tilde{\bar{\pi}}_{t})_{t\geq 0} is tight. By Prokhorov’s theorem, there exists a weakly converging subsequence, the limit of which is an invariant measure (as in the proof of the Krylov-Bogolyubov theorem). This proves the first claim. Now let us assume that there exists a unique invariant measure. Since any convergent subsequence of (π¯~t)t≥0(\tilde{\bar{\pi}}_{t})_{t\geq 0} has to converge to the same limit, and the sequence is tight, the second claim follows. ∎

By the results obtained in [45], uniqueness of the invariant measure is implied by certain regularity properties of the process. This leads to the following convenient criterion.

Corollary 16 (Regular couplings).

Let Assumption 2 be satisfied and consider a Feller coupling (X¯t)t≥0(\bar{X}_{t})_{t\geq 0}. If the corresponding transition functions (ρt​(x,⋅))t≥0,x∈E¯(\rho_{t}(x,\cdot))_{t\geq 0,x\in\bar{E}} are mutually absolutely continuous (i.e. if the process is regular), then (X¯t)t≥0(\bar{X}_{t})_{t\geq 0} is ergodic.

The measures πi\pi_{i}, as well as π¯Γ\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma} (for Γ∈𝒢0\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}^{0}) induce the usual Hilbert spaces L2​(πi)L^{2}(\pi_{i}) and L2​(π¯Γ)L^{2}(\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}) of square-integrable functions. A crucial role will be played furthermore by the corresponding subspaces of centred functions, defined by

L02​(π¯Γ)={f∈L2​(π¯Γ)|π¯Γ​(f)=0},L^{2}_{0}(\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma})=\{f\in L^{2}(\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma})\,|\,\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}(f)=0\}, (32)

and analogously for L02​(πi)L_{0}^{2}(\pi_{i}). Since any Feller process has a right-continuous version, the semigroups (S¯tΓ)t≥0(\bar{S}_{t}^{\Gamma})_{t\geq 0} as well as the corresponding generators (ℒ¯Γ,𝒟⁡(ℒ¯Γ))(\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma},\mathcal{D}(\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma})) have unique extensions to strongly continuous semigroups on L2​(π¯Γ)L^{2}(\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}) by Jensen’s inequality. Slightly abusing the notation, we will denote those semigroups and their generators by the same letters. Before moving on to a somewhat more explicit description of coupling operators, let us mention the following open question, related to Conjecture 11:

Conjecture 17.

The set 𝒢0\mathcal{G}^{0} is convex.

2.4 A general way of constructing coupling operators

In this section we describe an approach to construct coupling operators explicitly in applications. The particular form presented here is also theoretically important since some of the calculations in later sections depend on it (especially the proof of Theorem 47).

As in the previous section, we assume that the marginal processes are ergodic with respect to invariant measures πi\pi_{i} (see Assumption 2). Furthermore, let us assume that the generators ℒi\mathcal{L}_{i} can be written as

ℒi=−∑k=1Ki(Aki)∗Aki+Bi,\mathcal{L}_{i}=-\sum_{k=1}^{K_{i}}(A_{k}^{i})^{*}A_{k}^{i}+B^{i}, (33)

where (Aki)∗(A_{k}^{i})^{*} denotes the adjoint of AkiA_{k}^{i} in L2​(πi)L^{2}(\pi_{i}), and BiB^{i} is antisymmetric in L2​(πi)L^{2}(\pi_{i}). Clearly, this decomposition into symmetric and antisymmetric parts is always possible, and in many cases the operators AkiA_{k}^{i} and BiB^{i} can be chosen to have convenient forms. Note however that the decomposition (33) is not unique, since there are (infinitely) many ways of choosing the operators AkiA^{i}_{k}. A particular choice of decomposing the generators ℒi\mathcal{L}_{i} as in (33) hence essentially amounts to the choice of square-roots for the symmetric parts. We remark here that naturally Cc∞​(E¯)⊂𝒟⁡(Aki)C_{c}^{\infty}(\bar{E})\subset\mathcal{D}(A_{k}^{i}) and Cc∞​(E¯)⊂𝒟⁡(Bi)C_{c}^{\infty}(\bar{E})\subset\mathcal{D}(B^{i}) are implicitly assumed, authorising the computations in later sections. The following Lemma is essential for the construction in this subsection:

Lemma 18.

Let AkiA_{k}^{i} and BiB^{i} be given as in equation (33). Then

span⁡𝟏⊂ker⁡Aki,span⁡𝟏⊂ker⁡Bi,\Span\mathbf{1}\subset\ker A_{k}^{i},\quad\Span\mathbf{1}\subset\ker B^{i}, (34)

for all i∈{1,…,n},k∈{1,…​Ki}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\,k\in\{1,\ldots K_{i}\}.

Proof.

See [85, Proposition 2]. ∎

We may now set

Γ=∑(i,j,k,l)∈𝒥αi​j​k​l​(x1,…,xn)​Aki​Alj\Gamma=\sum_{(i,j,k,l)\in\mathcal{J}}\alpha_{ijkl}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})A_{k}^{i}A_{l}^{j} (35)

for appropriate measurable functions αi​j​k​l:E¯→ℝ\alpha_{ijkl}:\bar{E}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} and where we have introduced the set of admissible indices

𝒥={(i,j,k,l)∈ℕ4:1≤i,j≤n,i≠j,1≤k≤Ki, 1≤l≤Kj},\mathcal{J}=\{(i,j,k,l)\in\mathbb{N}^{4}:1\leq i,j\leq n,\,i\neq j,1\leq k\leq K_{i},\,1\leq l\leq K_{j}\}, (36)

associated to the decomposition (33). Applying Lemma 18, we see immediately that the first condition of Definition 6 is satisfied. The second condition will typically enforce certain bounds on the functions αi​j​k​l\alpha_{ijkl} via the positive maximum principle as well as regularity constraints if we are interested in Feller couplings. Those properties will have to be determined according to the particular form of the generators ℒi\mathcal{L}_{i}. Furthermore, whether Γ\Gamma as defined in (35) belongs to 𝒢0\mathcal{G}^{0} will also depend on the choice of the functions αi​j​k​l\alpha_{ijkl}.

It is not clear whether the construction presented in this section exhausts the class of coupling operators 𝒢\mathcal{G}. We present this problem as a conjecture:

Conjecture 19.

For i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, assume that we are given generators (ℒi,𝒟⁡(ℒi))(\mathcal{L}_{i},\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{L}_{i})) of ergodic Feller semigroups. Then there exist decompositions of the form (33) and a set of functions

𝒰={(αi​j​k​l)(i,j,k,l)∈𝒥:E¯→ℝ}\mathcal{U}=\{\left(\alpha_{ijkl}\right)_{(i,j,k,l)\in\mathcal{J}}:\bar{E}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\} (37)

such that

𝒢={Γ=∑(i,j,k,l)∈𝒥αi​j​k​lAkiAlj:αi​j​k​l∈𝒰}.\mathcal{G}=\left\{\Gamma=\sum_{(i,j,k,l)\in\mathcal{J}}\alpha_{ijkl}A_{k}^{i}A_{l}^{j}:\quad\alpha_{ijkl}\in\mathcal{U}\right\}. (38)

In the case when the underlying processes (Xti)t≥0(X^{i}_{t})_{t\geq 0} are ℝdi\mathbb{R}^{d_{i}}-valued (i.e. Ei=ℝdiE_{i}=\mathbb{R}^{d_{i}}) and have continuous paths almost surely, Courrège’s Theorem ([19, Theorem 0.1], see also [43, Section 4.5] for a more recent account) provides an explicit characterisation of Feller generators. If furthermore these processes are ergodic with respect to given invariant measures, the decomposition of their generators into symmetric and antisymmetric part can be made explicit (see [28, Theorem 1]). Combining these theorems, we obtain the following partial result:

Proposition 20.

Let Ei=ℝdiE_{i}=\mathbb{R}^{d_{i}} for positive integers di∈ℕd_{i}\in\mathbb{N} and assume that the processes (Xti)t≥0(X_{t}^{i})_{t\geq 0} are ergodic and solve the Itô SDEs

d​Xti=bi​(Xti)​d​t+2​σi​(Xti)​d​Wti,\mathrm{d}X_{t}^{i}=b^{i}(X_{t}^{i})\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}\sigma^{i}(X_{t}^{i})\,\mathrm{d}W_{t}^{i}, (39)

where bi∈C1​(ℝdi,ℝdi)b^{i}\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d_{i}},\mathbb{R}^{d_{i}}), σ∈C1​(ℝdi,ℝdi×mi)\sigma\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d_{i}},\mathbb{R}^{d_{i}\times m_{i}}), and (Wti)t≥0(W_{t}^{i})_{t\geq 0} are standard mim_{i}-dimensional Brownian motions. Then the conclusion of Conjecture 19 holds.

3 Examples of coupled processes

Here we will illustrate the framework developed in the last section with concrete examples. Throughout we consider the task of sampling from the measure

π⁡(d​x)=1Z​e−V⁡(x)​d​x,x∈ℝd,\pi(\mathrm{d}x)=\frac{1}{Z}e^{-V(x)}\mathrm{d}x,\quad x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, (40)

where V∈C∞​(ℝd)V\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is a potential satisfying

Z:=∫ℝde−V⁡(x)​𝑑x<∞.Z:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{-V(x)}\mathrm{d}x<\infty. (41)

3.1 Overdamped Langevin dynamics

Our first group of examples is concerned with the overdamped Langevin dynamics [68, Section 4.5]. Let us start with the one-dimensional case, already encountered in the introduction.

3.1.1 Two particles in one dimension

We consider n=2n=2 particles moving in dimension d=1d=1, each of them according to the dynamics

d​Xt=−V′​(Xt)​d​t+2​d​Wt.\mathrm{d}X_{t}=-V^{\prime}(X_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}W_{t}. (42)

Note that in order to precisely fit into our framework developed in the previous section, the process (Xt)t≥0(X_{t})_{t\geq 0} is required to be a Feller process according to Definition 1. This property can be guaranteed by imposing certain growth conditions on the potential VV, see [51, Proposition 5.9] and [58, Theorem 5.3.2, Example 5.3.3]. However, we wish to remark that the Feller property is not crucial in practice and dispensing with this regularity requirement still leads to perfectly well-defined couplings as will become clear in Lemma 22 below. The generator of (42) is given by

ℒ=−V′(x)∂x+∂x2=−∂x∗∂x,\mathcal{L}=-V^{\prime}(x)\partial_{x}+\partial_{x}^{2}=-\partial_{x}^{*}\partial_{x}, (43)

where the adjoint is taken in L2​(π)L^{2}(\pi). In particular, ℒ\mathcal{L} can naturally be written in the form (33), with A=∂xA=\partial_{x} and B=0B=0. To illustrate trivial couplings (see Example 10), consider first two independent identical copies of (42), denoted by (Xt,Yt)t≥0(X_{t},Y_{t})_{t\geq 0}, hence evolving according to the dynamics

d​Xt\displaystyle\mathrm{d}X_{t} =−V′​(Xt)​d​t+2​d​Wtx,\displaystyle=-V^{\prime}(X_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}W^{x}_{t}, (44a)
d​Yt\displaystyle\mathrm{d}Y_{t} =−V′​(Yt)​d​t+2​d​Wty,\displaystyle=-V^{\prime}(Y_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}W^{y}_{t}, (44b)

on the product space E¯=ℝ2\bar{E}=\mathbb{R}^{2}. Since for now the processes (Wtx)t≥0(W^{x}_{t})_{t\geq 0} and (Wty)t≥0(W^{y}_{t})_{t\geq 0} are supposed to be two independent standard Brownian motions, the generator of (44) is given by

ℒ¯0=ℒx+ℒy,\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}=\mathcal{L}_{x}+\mathcal{L}_{y}, (45)

with ℒx=−V′(x)∂x+∂x2=−∂x∗∂x\mathcal{L}_{x}=-V^{\prime}(x)\partial_{x}+\partial_{x}^{2}=-\partial_{x}^{*}\partial_{x} and ℒy=−V′(y)∂y+∂y2=−∂y∗∂y\mathcal{L}_{y}=-V^{\prime}(y)\partial_{y}+\partial_{y}^{2}=-\partial_{y}^{*}\partial_{y}, in agreement with Example 10, equation (27). The invariant measure of (44) is given by the product

π¯0=πx⊗πy=1Z2​e−(V⁡(x)+V⁡(y))​d​x​d​y.\bar{\pi}_{0}=\pi_{x}\otimes\pi_{y}=\frac{1}{Z^{2}}e^{-\left(V(x)+V(y)\right)}\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}y. (46)

Now let us consider nontrivial couplings. Following Section 2.4, we may set

Γ=2α(x,y)∂x∂y,\Gamma=2\alpha(x,y)\partial_{x}\partial_{y}, (47)

for an appropriate measurable function α:ℝ2→ℝ\alpha:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} (we have inserted a factor of 22 for convenience). According to Proposition 20, the set of operators of the form (47) exhausts the set of coupling operators 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Clearly, the first condition of Definition 6 is satisfied for this set of operators (this is already guaranteed by using the construction from Section 2.4). The second condition enforces

−1≤α⁡(x,y)≤1,for all ​x,y∈ℝ.-1\leq\alpha(x,y)\leq 1,\quad\mbox{for all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}. (48)

Indeed, observe that

ℒ¯Γ=ℒ¯0+Γ=∇zU​(z)⋅∇z+Q⁡(z):∇z∇z,\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}=\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}+\Gamma=\nabla_{z}U(z)\cdot\nabla_{z}+Q(z):\nabla_{z}\nabla_{z}, (49)

where z=(x,y)z=(x,y), U⁡(z)=U⁡(x,y)=V⁡(x)+V⁡(y)U(z)=U(x,y)=V(x)+V(y),

Q⁡(z)=Q⁡(x,y)=(1α⁡(x,y)α⁡(x,y)1),Q(z)=Q(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}1&\alpha(x,y)\\ \alpha(x,y)&1\end{pmatrix}, (50)

and where :: denotes the Frobenius inner product of matrices. According to Courrège’s theorem, ℒ¯Γ\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma} satisfies the positive maximum principle (required by the Hille-Yosida-Ray Theorem) only if Q⁡(z)Q(z) is nonnegative definite for every z∈ℝ2z\in\mathbb{R}^{2} . From this, we immediately deduce the constraint (48).

Remark 21.

We are deliberately vague about the regularity properties of α\alpha. If we restrict our attention to Feller processes, α\alpha certainly has to be at least continuous, and there are multiple results in the literature guaranteeing the Feller property under mild further assumptions on α\alpha, in particular, Hölder regularity [3, 58]. For a discussion of the martingale problem for generators with discontinuous coefficients see the recent preprint [49] and references therein. Note that even in this simple case, it is very challenging to characterise exactly the set 𝒢\mathcal{G} as introduced in Definition 6. In applications, however, the Feller property is not crucial. Lemma 22 below shows that measurability of α\alpha is sufficient to ensure that a reasonable coupled process can be constructed.

Assuming that (48) is satisfied, the dynamics induced by the generator (49) are (at least formally) given by

d​(XtYt)=(−V′​(Xt)−V′​(Yt))​d​t+2​G​(Xt,Yt)​(d​Wtxd​Wty),\mathrm{d}\begin{pmatrix}X_{t}\\ Y_{t}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-V^{\prime}(X_{t})\\ -V^{\prime}(Y_{t})\end{pmatrix}\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}G(X_{t},Y_{t})\begin{pmatrix}\mathrm{d}W^{x}_{t}\\ \mathrm{d}W^{y}_{t}\end{pmatrix}, (51)

where G⁡(x,y)​G​(x,y)T=Q⁡(x,y)G(x,y)G(x,y)^{T}=Q(x,y), for instance

G⁡(x,y)=(cos⁡β⁡(x,y)g⁡(x,y)​sin⁡β​(x,y)g⁡(x,y)​sin⁡β​(x,y)cos⁡β⁡(x,y)),G(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\beta(x,y)&g(x,y)\sin\beta(x,y)\\ g(x,y)\sin\beta(x,y)&\cos\beta(x,y)\end{pmatrix}, (52)

with β⁡(x,y)=12​arcsin⁡|α⁡(x,y)|\beta(x,y)=\frac{1}{2}\arcsin|\alpha(x,y)| and g⁡(x,y)=sgn⁡α⁡(x,y)g(x,y)=\sgn\alpha(x,y). We have chosen this parametrisation since it generalises readily to higher dimensions (see below). Let us stress that writing the dynamics in the form (51) is vital for applications, since it enables its simulation in a straightforward manner. The following lemma shows that the process constructed in this way is indeed a coupling in the sense of Definition 4. Furthermore, it turns out that only minimal regularity of α\alpha is required.

Lemma 22.

Let α\alpha be measurable. Then the dynamics (51) can be written as

d​(XtYt)=(−V′​(Xt)−V′​(Yt))​d​t+2​(d​Btxd​Bty),\mathrm{d}\begin{pmatrix}X_{t}\\ Y_{t}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-V^{\prime}(X_{t})\\ -V^{\prime}(Y_{t})\end{pmatrix}\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}\begin{pmatrix}\mathrm{d}B^{x}_{t}\\ \mathrm{d}B^{y}_{t}\end{pmatrix}, (53)

with two Brownian motions (Btx)t≥0(B^{x}_{t})_{t\geq 0} and (Bty)t≥0(B^{y}_{t})_{t\geq 0} that are in general not independent.

Proof.

The claim follows from applying Lemma 72 to the components of the SDE

(d​Btxd​Bty)=G​(d​Wtxd​Wty),\begin{pmatrix}\mathrm{d}B^{x}_{t}\\ \mathrm{d}B^{y}_{t}\end{pmatrix}=G\begin{pmatrix}\mathrm{d}W^{x}_{t}\\ \mathrm{d}W^{y}_{t}\end{pmatrix}, (54)

noting that Gx:=(g​cos⁡β​sin⁡β)G^{x}:=(g\cos\beta\,\sin\beta) and Gy:=(g​sin⁡β​cos⁡β)G^{y}:=(g\sin\beta\,\cos\beta) indeed satisfy condition (187) with N=1N=1 and M=2M=2. ∎

Note that the function α\alpha (equivalently the pair β\beta and gg) encodes the coupling between the Brownian motions (Btx)t≥0(B^{x}_{t})_{t\geq 0} and (Bty)t≥0(B^{y}_{t})_{t\geq 0}. The parameter β∈[0,π4]\beta\in[0,\frac{\pi}{4}] is related to the strength of the coupling, whereas g∈{−1,1}g\in\{-1,1\} is related to its direction. Indeed, if β≡0\beta\equiv 0, then (Btx)t≥0(B_{t}^{x})_{t\geq 0} and (Bty)t≥0(B_{t}^{y})_{t\geq 0} are independent (‘trivial coupling’, see (44) and Example 10). If β≡π4\beta\equiv\frac{\pi}{4} and g≡1g\equiv 1, then Btx=BtyB^{x}_{t}=B^{y}_{t} for t≥0t\geq 0, almost surely (‘synchronous coupling’). Likewise, if β≡π4\beta\equiv\frac{\pi}{4} and g≡−1g\equiv-1, then Btx=−BtyB^{x}_{t}=-B^{y}_{t} (‘mirror coupling’).

Remark 23 (Ergodic couplings).

If the bound (48) is satisfied with strict inequalities, then the generator (49) is elliptic, and hence, by Corollary 16, the coupled process is ergodic. Let us mention that this condition is not necessary for ergodicity. Indeed, consider the coupling operator Γ=−2∂x∂y\Gamma=-2\partial_{x}\partial_{y}, inducing the so-called ‘two-point motion’ [7], i.e. (Xt)t≥0(X_{t})_{t\geq 0} and (Yt)t≥0(Y_{t})_{t\geq 0} are driven by the same Brownian motion, only differing by their initial laws. Under mild regularity conditions (i.e. Lipschitz continuity of the coefficients), it can be shown that (Xt,Yt)t≥0(X_{t},Y_{t})_{t\geq 0} is ergodic with respect to π¯Γ=1Z​e−V⁡(x)​δx−y​(d​x​d​y)\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}=\frac{1}{Z}e^{-V(x)}\delta_{x-y}(\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}y), see for instance [55, Theorem 2.1].

3.1.2 The general case

Here, we will extend the discussion from the previous section to the general case of nn particles moving in dd dimensions, i.e. we are concerned with couplings of the dynamics

dXti=−∇V(Xti)dt+2dWti,i=1,…,n,\mathrm{d}X^{i}_{t}=-\nabla V(X^{i}_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}W^{i}_{t},\quad i=1,\ldots,n, (55)

the processes (Xti)t≥0(X_{t}^{i})_{t\geq 0} being ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}-valued. If the Brownian motions (Wti)t≥0(W_{t}^{i})_{t\geq 0} are independent, then the joint process (X¯t)t≥0=(Xt1,…,Xtn)t≥0(\bar{X}_{t})_{t\geq 0}=(X^{1}_{t},\ldots,X^{n}_{t})_{t\geq 0} is ergodic with respect to the product measure π¯0=⨂i=1nπi\bar{\pi}_{0}=\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n}\pi_{i} on ℝn​d\mathbb{R}^{nd} (see Example 10) and the corresponding generator is given by

ℒ¯0=∑i=1nℒi,ℒi=−∇V(xi)⋅∇xi+Δxi=−∑k=1d(∂ki)∗∂ki.\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}_{i},\quad\mathcal{L}_{i}=-\nabla V(x_{i})\cdot\nabla_{x_{i}}+\Delta_{x_{i}}=-\sum_{k=1}^{d}(\partial_{k}^{i})^{*}\partial_{k}^{i}. (56)

Here, ∂ki\partial_{k}^{i} denotes the derivative with respect to the kk-th component of xix_{i}, and the adjoints are taken in the spaces L2​(πi)L^{2}(\pi_{i}). Clearly, the generators ℒi\mathcal{L}_{i} are decomposed as in (33), with Aki=∂kiA_{k}^{i}=\partial_{k}^{i} and Bi=0B^{i}=0.

Remark 24.

Instead of (55), we can also consider the more general dynamics

dXti=−Qi(Xti)∇V(Xti)dt+(∇⋅Qi)(Xti)dt+Ji∇V(Xti)dt+2​Qi​(Xti)dWti,\mathrm{d}X^{i}_{t}=-Q_{i}(X^{i}_{t})\nabla V(X^{i}_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t+(\nabla\cdot Q_{i})(X^{i}_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t+J_{i}\nabla V(X_{t}^{i})\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2Q_{i}(X^{i}_{t})}\,\mathrm{d}W^{i}_{t}, (57)

with i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, Ji∈ℝskewd×dJ_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}_{\mathrm{skew}} being skew-symmetric matrices and Qi:ℝd→ℝsymd×dQ_{i}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}_{\mathrm{sym}} being positive definite matrix-valued functions, as discussed in [28, Section 2]. Note that in this case the processes (Xti)t≥0(X^{i}_{t})_{t\geq 0} are not copies of each other, since QiQ_{i} and JiJ_{i} may not be the same for different particles.

To construct nontrivial couplings, we may set

Γ=∑i,j=1,i≠jn∑k,l=1dαi​j​k​l∂ki∂lj\Gamma=\sum_{i,j=1,i\neq j}^{n}\sum_{k,l=1}^{d}\alpha_{ijkl}\partial_{k}^{i}\partial_{l}^{j} (58)

for appropriate66 6 Concerning the regularity of these functions, the discussion from the previous section applies, see in particular Remark 21. functions αi​j​k​l:ℝn​d→ℝ\alpha_{ijkl}:\mathbb{R}^{nd}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, following Section 2.4. Note that ∂ki∂lj\partial_{k}^{i}\partial_{l}^{j} is symmetric with respect to the interchange of indices (i,k)↔(j,l)(i,k)\leftrightarrow(j,l), and so we may assume that αi​j​k​l=αj​i​l​k\alpha_{ijkl}=\alpha_{jilk}. As in the one-dimensional case, the generator of the coupled system ℒ¯Γ=ℒ¯0+Γ\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}=\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}+\Gamma is a second order differential operator which we require to be (possibly degenerately) elliptic in order for the second condition of Definition 6 to be satisfied (again with reference to Courrège’s theorem).

To derive more easily verifiable conditions on the functions αi​j​k​l\alpha_{ijkl}, let us introduce a matrix-valued function (or matrix field) Q:(ℝd)n→ℝn​d×n​dQ:(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{nd\times nd} as follows. Firstly, it is helpful to view the target space of QQ as ℝn​d×n​d≡(ℝd×d)n×n\mathbb{R}^{nd\times nd}\equiv(\mathbb{R}^{d\times d})^{n\times n}, i.e. we think of Q⁡(x1,…,xn)Q(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) as an n×nn\times n-matrix the entries of which are themselves d×dd\times d matrices. In other words, Qi​j​(x1,…,xn)Q_{ij}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) is a d×dd\times d matrix for every pair (i,j)∈{1,…,n}2(i,j)\in\{1,\ldots,n\}^{2}. The matrix field QQ can then be defined by

Qi​j​(x1,…,xn)={Id×d,i=j,αi​j(x1,…,xn),i≠j,Q_{ij}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=\begin{cases}I_{d\times d},\quad&i=j,\\ \alpha_{ij}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}),\quad&i\neq j,\end{cases} (59)

where αi​j​(x1,…,xn)∈ℝd×d\alpha_{ij}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} denotes the matrix with entries (αi​j​k​l​(x1,…,xn))k,l=1,…,d(\alpha_{ijkl}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}))_{k,l=1,\ldots,d}. Note that Q⁡(x1,…,xn)Q(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) as defined in (59) is symmetric as a matrix in ℝn​d×n​d\mathbb{R}^{nd\times nd} by our assumption that αi​j​k​l=αj​i​l​k\alpha_{ijkl}=\alpha_{jilk}.

Remark 25.

The matrices Qi​jQ_{ij} can now be thought of as describing the coupling between the particles ii and jj.

As in the one-dimensional case, the generator of the fully coupled system can be written as

ℒ¯Γ=ℒ¯0+Γ=∇zU​(z)⋅∇z+Q⁡(z):∇z∇z,\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}=\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}+\Gamma=\nabla_{z}U(z)\cdot\nabla_{z}+Q(z):\nabla_{z}\nabla_{z}, (60)

introducing the notation z≡(x1,…,xn)∈ℝn​d×n​dz\equiv(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{nd\times nd} and U⁡(z)=∑i=1nV⁡(xi)U(z)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}V(x_{i}). To make the connection to SDEs and arrive at a description analogous to (51), let us consider matrix fields G:(ℝd)n→(ℝd×d)n×nG:(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{n}\rightarrow(\mathbb{R}^{d\times d})^{n\times n} satisfying

∑j=1nGi​j​(x1,…,xn)​Gi​j​(x1,…,xn)T=Id×d,\sum_{j=1}^{n}G_{ij}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})G_{ij}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})^{T}=I_{d\times d}, (61)

for all i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n. Here the transposition T is taken in ℝd×d\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}. Note that matrix fields of this form give rise to the matrix fields Q:(ℝd)n→ℝn​d×n​dQ:(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{nd\times nd} defined in (59) via Q=G​GTQ=GG^{T} (where the transposition is taken in ℝn​d×n​d\mathbb{R}^{nd\times nd}).

Remark 26.

The advantage of constructing the coupling in terms of the matrix field GG is that pointwise positive semi-definiteness of QQ is automatically satisfied. A practical way to fulfil the constraint (61) is to choose matrix fields gi​j:(ℝd)n→ℝd×dg_{ij}:(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} that are orthogonal pointwise, i.e.

gi​j​(x1,…,xn)​gi​j​(x1,…,xn)T=gi​j​(x1,…,xn)T​gi​j​(x1,…,xn)=Id×d,g_{ij}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})g_{ij}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})^{T}=g_{ij}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})^{T}g_{ij}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=I_{d\times d}, (62)

for all i,j=1,…,ni,j=1,\ldots,n and (x1,…,xn)∈(ℝd)n(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{n}, as well as weights wi​j:(ℝd)n→ℝw_{ij}:(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} satisfying

∑j=1nwi​j2​(x1,…,xn)=1,\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{ij}^{2}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=1, (63)

for all i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n. Then, setting Gi​j=wi​j​gi​jG_{ij}=w_{ij}g_{ij}, condition (61) holds. Intuitively, the orthogonal matrices gi​jg_{ij} encode the coupling between particle ii and jj through a rotation of the noise. The weights wi​jw_{ij} can be interpreted as the relative coupling strengths between the particles. Observe that both gi​jg_{ij} and wi​jw_{ij} may depend on (x1,…,xn)(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}), i.e. on the locations of all the particles. This construction is a direct generalisation of (52).

Assuming G​GT=QGG^{T}=Q, the dynamics associated to the generator (60) is (again, at least formally) given by

dXti=−∇V(Xti)dt+2∑j=1nGi​j(Xt1,…,Xtn)dWtj,i=1,…,n,\mathrm{d}X_{t}^{i}=-\nabla V(X_{t}^{i})\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}\sum_{j=1}^{n}G_{ij}(X_{t}^{1},\ldots,X_{t}^{n})\,\mathrm{d}W_{t}^{j},\quad i=1,\ldots,n, (64)

where ((Wtj)t≥0)j=1n\left((W_{t}^{j})_{t\geq 0}\right)_{j=1}^{n} are assumed to be independent standard Brownian motions. As in the one-dimensional case, we have the following lemma:

Lemma 27.

There exist ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}-valued standard Brownian motions ((Btj)t≥0)j=1n\left((B_{t}^{j})_{t\geq 0}\right)_{j=1}^{n}, not necessarily independent, such that the dynamics (64) can be written as

dXti=−∇V(Xti)dt+2dBti,i=1,…,n.\mathrm{d}X_{t}^{i}=-\nabla V(X_{t}^{i})\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}B_{t}^{i},\quad i=1,\ldots,n. (65)
Proof.

The argument is identical to the one used in the proof of Lemma 22. ∎

Concerning the ergodicity of couplings, we have similar findings to those of Remark 23. If the matrix field (59) is positive definite at every point (i.e. the generator (60) is elliptic), then Corollary 16 implies that the coupled process is ergodic. An example of nonergodic couplings can be found in [55, Section 3.1].

For fixed γ>0\gamma>0 (‘friction’) and symmetric positive definite M∈ℝsymd×dM\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}_{\mathrm{sym}} (‘mass’), the dynamics

It is also possible to couple different types of dynamics (such as overdamped and underdamped Langevin dynamics). For instance, consider the generators

3.3 The zigzag process

In recent years, there has been a growing interest in using piecewise deterministic Markov processes (PDMPs) [23] in the context of sampling problems. These are processes that move deterministically between random events, usually along the trajectories of an ODE. At those events, a random transition (e.g. a ‘jump’) occurs. Both the deterministic dynamics as well as the random transitions can be chosen with a great deal of flexibility, resulting in a range of possible PDMP algorithms. Let us mention here the bouncy particle sampler (BPS) [15], the zigzag sampler [10], randomised Hamiltonian Monte Carlo [14], and event-chain Monte Carlo techniques [60, 61]. The recent papers [33] and [83] provide good overviews in a general framework.

The objective of this section is to show how the framework from Section 2 can be employed in the construction of coupled samplers from piecewise deterministic Markov processes, using the example of the zigzag process. For ease of exposition, we furthermore restrict our attention to the one-dimensional case. The treatment here follows [10] and [11] in style and notation.

The state space under consideration is E=ℝ×{−1,+1}E=\mathbb{R}\times\{-1,+1\}, and the generator of the zigzag process reads

ℒ​f​(x,θ)=θ​∂xf⁡(x,θ)+λ⁡(x,θ)​(f⁡(x,−θ)−f⁡(x,θ)),f∈Cc∞​(E),\mathcal{L}f(x,\theta)=\theta\partial_{x}f(x,\theta)+\lambda(x,\theta)\left(f(x,-\theta)-f(x,\theta)\right),\quad f\in C_{c}^{\infty}(E), (80)

where the switching rate λ\lambda is given by

λ⁡(x,θ)=max⁡(0,θ​V′​(x))+γ⁡(x).\lambda(x,\theta)=\max(0,\theta V^{\prime}(x))+\gamma(x). (81)

Here, γ:ℝ→ℝ≥0\gamma:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} is a nonnegative continuous function, called the excess switching rate. Roughly speaking, the zigzag process moves along straight lines in the direction determined by θ∈{−1,1}\theta\in\{-1,1\}. At random times a switch occurs, i.e. θ\theta is replaced by −θ-\theta. Those events are sampled according to the switching rate λ\lambda, i.e. at a point (x,θ)∈E(x,\theta)\in E, the probability for the switch θ↦−θ\theta\mapsto-\theta in the time span [t,t+ε][t,t+\varepsilon] is given by λ⁡(x,t)​ε+o⁡(ε)\lambda(x,t)\varepsilon+o(\varepsilon). For more details on the construction and simulation of zigzag processes we refer the reader to [9] an [10], as well as to [23] for more general piecewise deterministic Markov processes. According to [9, Proposition 1] and [83, Appendix B.2], the zigzag process satisfies the Feller property; for more general piecewise deterministic Markov processes this topic has been studied in [24, see Theorem 27.6]. The measure

π=12​Z​e−V⁡(x)​d​x⊗(δ−1+δ+1)\pi=\frac{1}{2Z}e^{-V(x)}\mathrm{d}x\otimes(\delta_{-1}+\delta_{+1}) (82)

is invariant, and, under some additional assumptions77 7 See [9] and [11]. Let us mention in particular that ergodicity is guaranteed whenever the excess switching rate γ\gamma is strictly positive., ergodic. The generator (80) can be decomposed in the form

ℒ=−A∗​A+B,\mathcal{L}=-A^{*}A+B, (83)

where

A=(14|V′|+12γ)1/2(R−1),B=θ∂x+12θV′(R−1),A=\left(\frac{1}{4}|V^{\prime}|+\frac{1}{2}\gamma\right)^{1/2}(R-1),\quad B=\theta\partial_{x}+\frac{1}{2}\theta V^{\prime}(R-1), (84)

and the ‘flip operator’ RR is given by

(R​f)​(x,θ)=f⁡(x,−θ),f∈Cc∞​(E¯).\quad(Rf)(x,\theta)=f(x,-\theta),\quad f\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\bar{E}). (85)

A short calculation shows that indeed BB is antisymmetric in L2​(π)L^{2}(\pi), whereas AA is symmetric.

To construct a coupled sampler from two zigzag processes, let us introduce the following notation: We consider the state space E¯=ℝ2×{−1,+1}2\bar{E}=\mathbb{R}^{2}\times\{-1,+1\}^{2}, denoting its elements by (x,y,θx,θy)(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y}). Furthermore, we will make use of the flip operators

(Rx​f)​(x,y,θx,θy)=f⁡(x,y,−θx,θy),(Ry​f)​(x,y,θx,θy)=f⁡(x,y,θx,−θy).(R_{x}f)(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y})=f(x,y,-\theta_{x},\theta_{y}),\quad(R_{y}f)(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y})=f(x,y,\theta_{x},-\theta_{y}). (86)

Following Section 2.4, let us set

Γ=α⁡(x,y,θx,θy)​(Rx−1)​(Ry−1),\Gamma=\alpha(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y})(R_{x}-1)(R_{y}-1), (87)

for an appropriate function α:E¯→ℝ\alpha:\bar{E}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, i.e. Γ\Gamma acts as

(Γ​f)\displaystyle(\Gamma f) (x,y,θx,θy)=α(x,y,θx,θy)⋅\displaystyle(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y})=\alpha(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y})\cdot (88)
⋅(f⁡(x,y,θx,θy)−f⁡(x,y,−θx,θy)−f⁡(x,y,θx,−θy)+f⁡(x,y,−θx,−θy))\displaystyle\cdot\left(f(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y})-f(x,y,-\theta_{x},\theta_{y})-f(x,y,\theta_{x},-\theta_{y})+f(x,y,-\theta_{x},-\theta_{y})\right)

on test functions f∈Cc∞​(E¯)f\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\bar{E}). Note that Γ\Gamma vanishes on functions that either depend on only xx and θx\theta_{x} or only on yy and θy\theta_{y}. The next task is to obtain bounds on α\alpha that ensure that the second condition in Definition 6 is satisfied. To this end, let us expand

(ℒ¯Γ​f)​(x,y,θx,θy)=\displaystyle(\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}f)(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y})=\, (ℒx+ℒy+Γ)​f​(x,y,θx,θy)\displaystyle(\mathcal{L}_{x}+\mathcal{L}_{y}+\Gamma)f(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y}) (89a)
=\displaystyle=\, θx​∂xf⁡(x,y,θx,θy)+θy​∂yf⁡(x,y,θx,θy)\displaystyle\theta_{x}\partial_{x}f(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y})+\theta_{y}\partial_{y}f(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y}) (89b)
−(λ⁡(x,θx)+λ⁡(y,θy)−α⁡(x,y,θx,θy))​f​(x,y,θx,θy)\displaystyle-\left(\lambda(x,\theta_{x})+\lambda(y,\theta_{y})-\alpha(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y})\right)f(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y}) (89c)
+(λ⁡(x,θx)−α⁡(x,y,θx,θy))​f​(x,y,−θx,θy)\displaystyle+\left(\lambda(x,\theta_{x})-\alpha(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y})\right)f(x,y,-\theta_{x},\theta_{y}) (89d)
+(λ⁡(y,θy)−α⁡(x,y,θx,θy))​f​(x,y,θx,−θy)\displaystyle+\left(\lambda(y,\theta_{y})-\alpha(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y})\right)f(x,y,\theta_{x},-\theta_{y}) (89e)
+α⁡(x,y,θx,θy)​f​(x,y,−θx,−θy).\displaystyle+\alpha(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y})f(x,y,-\theta_{x},-\theta_{y}). (89f)

For (89) to be the generator of a Markov process (in particular, for it to satisfy the positive maximum principle), the following inequalities have to be satified:

λ⁡(x,θx)+λ⁡(y,θy)−α⁡(x,y,θx,θy)\displaystyle\lambda(x,\theta_{x})+\lambda(y,\theta_{y})-\alpha(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y}) ≥0,\displaystyle\geq 0, (90a)
λ⁡(x,θx)−α⁡(x,y,θx,θy)\displaystyle\lambda(x,\theta_{x})-\alpha(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y}) ≥0,\displaystyle\geq 0, (90b)
λ⁡(y,θy)−α⁡(x,y,θx,θy)\displaystyle\lambda(y,\theta_{y})-\alpha(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y}) ≥0,\displaystyle\geq 0, (90c)
α⁡(x,y,θx,θy)\displaystyle\alpha(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y}) ≥0,(x,y,θx,θy)∈E¯.\displaystyle\geq 0,\quad\quad(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y})\in\bar{E}. (90d)

These conditions can be interpreted as saying that the transition probabilities for the coupled piecewise deterministic Markov process cannot be negative. Clearly, the conditions (90) are equivalent to

0≤α⁡(x,y,θx,θy)≤min⁡(λ⁡(x,θx),λ⁡(y,θy)),(x,y,θx,θy)∈E¯.0\leq\alpha(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y})\leq\min\left(\lambda(x,\theta_{x}),\lambda(y,\theta_{y})\right),\quad(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y})\in\bar{E}. (91)

Let us briefly comment on the dynamical behaviour that the coupling operator (88) introduces. As can be seen from (89f), α\alpha is connected to ‘double flips’, i.e. the event that both particles change their directions at the same time. Setting α\alpha to either the lower or the upper bound in (91) will either discourage or encourage those double flips. As in the case of the overdamped and underdamped Langevin dynamics, the coupling behaviour (encoded in α\alpha) is allowed to depend on the point (x,y,θx,θy)∈E¯(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y})\in\bar{E}. We also remark that the process generated by ℒ¯Γ\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma} as in (89) can be simulated conveniently by using the methods summarised in [9, Appendix B].

Remark 31.

The construction in this section can be generalised to couplings of multiple zigzag processes in arbitrary dimensions by following a similar approach to the one taken in Section 3.1.

4 Asymptotic variance and optimal transport

In the following we analyse the asymptotic variance associated to estimators based on coupled processes (Section 4.1) and connect the result to the theory of optimal transportation (Section 4.2).

4.1 A central limit theorem for coupled processes

The objective of this section is to establish a central limit theorem characterising the convergence in (8) and to find an expression for the associated asymptotic variance in terms of ergodic coupling operators Γ∈𝒢0\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}^{0} and invariant measures π¯Γ\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}. In particular, our aim is to compare between estimators based on couplings (as in (8)) and the one-particle estimators (30). Naturally, Assumption 2 is still in force. Moreover, let us assume the following:

Assumption 3 (Invertibility of the one-particle generators).

The generators ℒi\mathcal{L}_{i} are invertible on L02​(πi)L_{0}^{2}(\pi_{i}), i.e. for all f∈L02​(πi)f\in L_{0}^{2}(\pi_{i}) there exists ϕ∈𝒟⁡(ℒi)∩L02​(πi)\phi\in\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{L}_{i})\cap L_{0}^{2}(\pi_{i}) such that

−ℒi​ϕ=f.-\mathcal{L}_{i}\phi=f. (92)

It is well-known that the validity of the foregoing assumption is guaranteed by sufficiently fast decay of the semigroups (Sti)t≥0(S_{t}^{i})_{t\geq 0} in L2​(πi)L^{2}(\pi_{i}), see for instance [46]. In the following, let us fix observables of interest fi∈L02​(πi)f_{i}\in L_{0}^{2}(\pi_{i}) and denote the corresponding solutions to the Poisson equations (92) by ϕi\phi_{i}. Supposing X0i∼πiX^{i}_{0}\sim\pi_{i}, Assumption 3 implies the central limit theorems

T​(1T​∫0Tfi​(Xti)​𝑑t−πi​(fi))→T→∞𝑑𝒩⁡(0,2​σfi2),\sqrt{T}\left(\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}f_{i}(X^{i}_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t-\pi_{i}(f_{i})\right)\xrightarrow[T\rightarrow\infty]{d}\mathcal{N}(0,2\sigma_{f_{i}}^{2}), (93)

where the asymptotic variances are given by

σfi2=⟨fi,ϕi⟩L2​(πi),\sigma_{f_{i}}^{2}=\langle f_{i},\phi_{i}\rangle_{L^{2}(\pi_{i})}, (94)

see [8, 46].

We will now establish a similar central limit theorem for the coupled process (X¯t)t≥0(\bar{X}_{t})_{t\geq 0} induced by ergodic coupling operators Γ∈𝒢0\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}^{0} and associated to extended observables of the form

F=1n​∑i=1nfi.F=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}. (95)
Theorem 32.

Central limit theorem for coupled processes. Let Assumption 3 be satisfied and assume that Γ∈𝒢0\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}^{0}. Furthermore, let X¯0∼π¯Γ\bar{X}_{0}\sim\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}. Then

T​(1T​∫0TF⁡(X¯t)​𝑑t−π¯Γ​(F))→T→∞𝑑𝒩⁡(0,2​σF2).\sqrt{T}\left(\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}F(\bar{X}_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t-\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}(F)\right)\xrightarrow[T\rightarrow\infty]{d}\mathcal{N}(0,2\sigma_{F}^{2}). (96)

The asymptotic variance σF2\sigma_{F}^{2} is given by

σF2=1n2​∑i=1nσfi2−∫E¯ℒ¯0​ξ​d​π¯Γ,\sigma_{F}^{2}=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{f_{i}}^{2}-\int_{\bar{E}}\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}\xi\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}, (97)

where

ξ=1n2​∑i<jϕi​ϕj,\xi=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i<j}\phi_{i}\phi_{j}, (98)

the functions (ϕi)i=1n(\phi_{i})_{i=1}^{n} being the solutions to the Poisson equations (92).

Remark 33.

Note that in the case of the trivial coupling Γ=𝟎\Gamma=\mathbf{0} (see Example 10), we have that

∫E¯ℒ¯0​ξ​d​π¯0=0,\int_{\bar{E}}\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}\xi\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{0}=0, (99)

since π¯0\bar{\pi}_{0} is the invariant measure associated to the process generated by ℒ¯0\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}. Therefore in this case, we obtain the result that the asymptotic variance σF2\sigma_{F}^{2} is given by the arithmetic mean of the asymptotic variances σfi2\sigma_{f_{i}}^{2} of the one-particle processes, divided by nn. This result is expected, since the computational cost of computing the evolution of the processes (Xti)t≥0(X^{i}_{t})_{t\geq 0} is likewise increased by a factor of nn.

Remark 34.

Observe furthermore that

∫E¯ℒ¯Γ​ξ​d​π¯Γ=0,\int_{\bar{E}}\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}\xi\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}=0, (100)

hence using ℒ¯Γ=ℒ¯0+Γ\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}=\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}+\Gamma we can equivalently express the asymptotic variance as

σF2=1n2​∑i=1nσfi2+∫E¯Γ​ξ​d​π¯Γ.\sigma_{F}^{2}=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{f_{i}}^{2}+\int_{\bar{E}}\Gamma\xi\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}. (101)
Proof of Theorem 32.

First observe that by the fact that π¯Γ\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma} is a coupling of (πi)i=1n(\pi_{i})_{i=1}^{n}, we have that π¯Γ​(F)=0\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}(F)=0. The Poisson equation
