Again, the condition π¯Γ​(Φ)=0\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}(\Phi)=0 is satisfied by the coupling property of π¯Γ\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}. Using [8, Theorem 2.1], we see that the central limit theorem (96) holds with asymptotic variance

σF2=⟨F,Φ⟩L2​(π¯Γ).\sigma_{F}^{2}=\langle F,\Phi\rangle_{L^{2}(\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma})}. (104)

Expanding the above yields

σF2\displaystyle\sigma_{F}^{2} =\displaystyle= ∫E¯(1n​∑i=1nfi)​(1n​∑j=1nϕj)​d​π¯Γ=1n2​∑i=1n∫E¯fi​ϕi​d​π¯Γ+1n2​∑i,j=1i≠jn∫E¯fi​ϕj​d​π¯Γ\displaystyle\int_{\bar{E}}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}\right)\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\phi_{j}\right)\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\int_{\bar{E}}f_{i}\phi_{i}\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}+\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j=1\\ i\neq j\end{subarray}}^{n}\int_{\bar{E}}f_{i}\phi_{j}\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}
=\displaystyle= 1n2​∑i=1nσfi2−∫E¯ℒ¯0​ξ​d​π¯Γ,\displaystyle\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{f_{i}}^{2}-\int_{\bar{E}}\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}\xi\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma},

where in the last equation we used the fact that π¯Γ\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma} has marginal πi\pi_{i} in the ii-th coordinate, expression (94), as well as the definition of ξ\xi in (98). ∎

4.2 Connections to the theory of optimal transportation

In this section we will always assume that Assumption 3 is satisfied, so that the central limit theorems from the previous section hold. Theorem 32 then shows that, in order to reduce the asymptotic variance, we are led to the problem of minimising the expression

∫E¯(−ℒ¯0​ξ)​d​π¯Γ.\int_{\bar{E}}(-\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}\xi)\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}.

Remarkably, this expression depends on Γ\Gamma through the measure π¯Γ\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma} only88 8 Another way of saying this is that the map Γ↦σF2\Gamma\mapsto\sigma_{F}^{2} factors through the map Γ↦π¯Γ\Gamma\mapsto\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}, i.e. with respect to the asymptotic variance, no information is lost by considering only the invariant measure of the joint process.. We provide a sketch of this situation in Figure 1.

Since π¯Γ\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma} has fixed marginals (i.e. they do not depend on Γ\Gamma), this task is very reminiscent of the Kantorovich problem [86, Chapter 1] appearing in the theory of optimal transportation [84, 86]. To make this connection more precise, let us introduce the following terminology:

Definition 35 (Admissible couplings).

The set of couplings of the marginal invariant measures (πi)i=1n(\pi_{i})_{i=1}^{n} will be denoted by 𝒞\mathcal{C}. A coupling π¯∈𝒞\bar{\pi}\in\mathcal{C} is called admissible, if it arises as the invariant measure of an ergodically coupled process, i.e. if there exists Γ∈𝒢0\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}^{0} such that

∫E¯ℒ¯Γ​f​𝑑π¯=0,\int_{\bar{E}}\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}f\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}=0, (106)

for all f∈𝒟⁡(ℒ¯Γ)f\in\mathcal{D}(\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}). The set of admissible measures will be denoted by 𝒞0\mathcal{C}^{0}, or, stressing the dependence on the marginal measures, by 𝒞0​(π1,…,πn)\mathcal{C}^{0}(\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{n}).

Our aim in this section can be summarised in the following form, only replacing 𝒞\mathcal{C} by the subset 𝒞0\mathcal{C}^{0} in the standard formulation of the Kantorovich problem:

Problem 1.

For a fixed cost function c∈Cb​(E¯)c\in C_{b}(\bar{E}), find π¯∈𝒞0\bar{\pi}\in\mathcal{C}^{0} such that

π¯∈arg​minπ¯∈𝒞0∫E¯cdπ¯.\bar{\pi}\in\argmin_{\bar{\pi}\in\mathcal{C}^{0}}\int_{\bar{E}}c\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}. (107)

Equivalently, find minimisers of the function

𝒢0→ℝ,Γ↦∫E¯c​d​π¯Γ.\mathcal{G}^{0}\rightarrow\mathbb{R},\quad\Gamma\mapsto\int_{\bar{E}}c\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}. (108)
Remark 36.

As already pointed out, setting c=−ℒ¯0​ξ,c=-\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}\xi, with ξ\xi as defined in (98), is equivalent to the problem of optimising the asymptotic variance for a particular observable. Other choices for cc might be of interest. For instance, one might aim to optimise the asymptotic variance across a set of observables simultaneously. In this case, it seems reasonable to consider cost functions of the form c=∑jcjc=\sum_{j}c_{j}, where cjc_{j} is the cost function associated with the jjth observable. Assuming that all the particles evolve in the same state space EE, another natural objective would be to maximise the average distance of the particles at equilibrium, leading to a cost function of the type

c(x1,…,xn)=−∑i,j=1i≠jnd(xi,xj),c(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j=1\\ i\neq j\end{subarray}}^{n}d(x_{i},x_{j}), (109)

for some metric dd on EE. More generally, for some function g:ℝ→ℝg:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} it might be worthwhile to consider

c(x1,…,xn)=−∑i,j=1i≠jng(d(xi,xj)).c(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j=1\\ i\neq j\end{subarray}}^{n}g(d(x_{i},x_{j})). (110)

A cost function of this type would be reasonable if one aims to use the empirical measure of an ensemble of particles in order to precondition the dynamics (see [52]), in which case the particles should neither be too close nor too far away from each other. We emphasize that since in our framework the marginal processes are held fixed, our results are not directly applicable to the algorithm presented in [52]. However, we expect that the results might be generalised to this context.

Let us also remark that the assumption c∈Cb​(E¯)c\in C_{b}(\bar{E}) is mainly for technical convenience and both the continuity and the boundedness assumption can be weakened. Since we are interested is situations where the process (X¯)t≥0(\bar{X})_{t\geq 0} takes values in a compact set with high probability (i.e. the target measures πi\pi_{i} are concentrated in a compact set), boundedness of cc is not a severe restriction.

Remark 37.

Clearly, it holds that

infπ¯∈𝒞0∫E¯c​𝑑π¯≥infπ¯∈𝒞∫E¯c​𝑑π¯,\inf_{\bar{\pi}\in\mathcal{C}^{0}}\int_{\bar{E}}c\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}\geq\inf_{\bar{\pi}\in\mathcal{C}}\int_{\bar{E}}c\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}, (111)

so the solutions to the usual optimal transport problems provide lower bounds for Problem 1.

In the Kantorovich formulation, the cost function cc is often induced by a distance (for instance c⁡(x,y)=(d⁡(x,y))pc(x,y)=(d(x,y))^{p} for n=2n=2, 1≤p<∞1\leq p<\infty), penalising couplings that put probability mass on pairs of points (x,y)(x,y) where xx and yy are far apart from each other (hence the name optimal transport). In the setting of MCMC (in particular in the context of variance reduction), it is plausible to encourage the particles to stay away from each other, leading to sample diversity and improved exploration of the state space. In this respect, our setting bears certain similarities with the use of optimal transport problems in functional density theory, see [18].

The set 𝒞0\mathcal{C}^{0} depends on the generators ℒi\mathcal{L}_{i}. Furthermore, 𝒞0\mathcal{C}^{0} is a strict subset of 𝒞\mathcal{C}. The support of an ergodic invariant measure for a Markov process with continuous paths is necessarily connected, for instance, while in general the support of a coupling is not. The following example illustrates that 𝒞0\mathcal{C}^{0} is indeed usually significantly smaller than 𝒞\mathcal{C}:

Example 38 (The set 𝒞0\mathcal{C}^{0} contains only few singular measures).

Consider the setting from Section 3.1.1, i.e. two particles moving in one dimension according to overdamped Langevin dynamics. Let us fix a coupling Γ∈𝒢0\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}^{0} and assume that the invariant measure π¯Γ\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma} is supported on the zero set of a smooth function H:E¯→ℝH:\bar{E}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} with nowhere vanishing gradient, i.e.

suppπ¯Γ⊆{(x,y)∈E¯:H(x,y)=0}.\supp\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}\subseteq\{(x,y)\in\bar{E}:\quad H(x,y)=0\}. (112)

This implies that π¯Γ\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma} is supported on a submanifold of E¯\bar{E} and is hence necessarily singular with respect to the Lebesgue measure. Frequently, optimisers of standard optimal transport problems are of this type (see for instance [59, Theorem 1.2]). Itô’s formula implies that

H(X¯t)=H(X¯0)+∫0t(GT∇H)(X¯s)⋅dWs+∫0t(ℒ¯ΓH)(X¯s)ds,t≥0,H(\bar{X}_{t})=H(\bar{X}_{0})+\int_{0}^{t}(G^{T}\nabla H)(\bar{X}_{s})\cdot\mathrm{d}W_{s}+\int_{0}^{t}(\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}H)(\bar{X}_{s})\,\mathrm{d}s,\quad t\geq 0, (113)

where GG is given in (52). Choosing the initial condition X¯0∼π¯Γ\bar{X}_{0}\sim\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma} results in H⁡(X¯t)=H⁡(X¯0)=0H(\bar{X}_{t})=H(\bar{X}_{0})=0 almost surely, for all t≥0t\geq 0. It then follows that both of the remaining integral terms individually have to be zero (owing to the decomposition into martingale and bounded variation part). The quadratic variation of the martingale part is given by

∫0tw⁡(X¯s)​𝑑s,w=(∂xH)2+4​cos⁡β​sin⁡β⋅(∂xH)​(∂yH)+(∂yH)2.\int_{0}^{t}w(\bar{X}_{s})\,\mathrm{d}s,\quad w=(\partial_{x}H)^{2}+4\cos\beta\sin\beta\cdot(\partial_{x}H)(\partial_{y}H)+(\partial_{y}H)^{2}. (114)

Since the quadratic variation has be to be zero for all t≥0t\geq 0, it follows that ∂xH=±∂yH\partial_{x}H=\pm\partial_{y}H on supp⁡π¯Γ\supp\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}. Since HH is smooth with nonvanishing gradient, it turns out that supp⁡π¯Γ\supp\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma} is contained in either one of the diagonals x=yx=y or x=−yx=-y, in fact either π¯Γ=1Z​e−V⁡(x)​δx−y​(d​x​d​y)\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}=\frac{1}{Z}e^{-V(x)}\delta_{x-y}(\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}y) or π¯Γ=1Z​e−V⁡(x)​δx+y​(d​x​d​y)\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}=\frac{1}{Z}e^{-V(x)}\delta_{x+y}(\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}y), noting that the latter is only possible if VV has the symmetry property V⁡(x)=V⁡(−x)V(x)=V(-x). We conclude that, at least in the example considered here, 𝒞0\mathcal{C}^{0} contains only very few singular measures.

From the theory of optimal transportation it is known that solutions of the Kantorovich problem are typically quite singular, in the sense that they are supported on small sets (see for instance [59, Theorem 1.2]). As Example 38 shows, these measures often do not belong to 𝒞0\mathcal{C}^{0}. The aim of this section is to show a similar singularity property for Problem 1. Informally speaking, we will see that under reasonable conditions, the optimisers of (108) are not attained for coupling operators in the interior of 𝒢0\mathcal{G}^{0}. To make this statement precise, let us fix the decompositions

ℒi=−∑k=1Ki(Aki)∗Aki+Bi\mathcal{L}_{i}=-\sum_{k=1}^{K_{i}}(A_{k}^{i})^{*}A_{k}^{i}+B^{i} (115)

of the underlying generators (see Section 2.4) and lay the focus on coupling operators of the form (35), denoting this set by 𝒢⁡(A)\mathcal{G}(A):

𝒢(A)={Γ=∑(i,j,k,l)∈𝒥αi​j​k​lAkiAlj:αi​j​k​l:E¯→ℝ}∩𝒢,\mathcal{G}(A)=\left\{\Gamma=\sum_{(i,j,k,l)\in\mathcal{J}}\alpha_{ijkl}A_{k}^{i}A_{l}^{j}:\quad\alpha_{ijkl}:\bar{E}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\right\}\cap\mathcal{G}, (116)

where we recall the set 𝒥\mathcal{J} of admissible indices, defined in (36). We wish to stress however that the distinction between 𝒢⁡(A)\mathcal{G}(A) and 𝒢\mathcal{G} is often obsolete (see Proposition 20). The subset of ergodic coupling operators will similarly be denoted by 𝒢0​(A)\mathcal{G}^{0}(A). Let us now introduce the ‘tangent space’ to 𝒢⁡(A)\mathcal{G}(A):

T​𝒢​(A)={∑(i,j,k,l)∈𝒥αi​j​k​l​Aki​Alj|αi​j​k​l∈Cc∞​(E¯)}.T\mathcal{G}(A)=\left\{\sum_{(i,j,k,l)\in\mathcal{J}}\alpha_{ijkl}A_{k}^{i}A_{l}^{j}\,|\,\alpha_{ijkl}\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\bar{E})\right\}. (117)
Remark 39.

The definition of T​𝒢​(A)T\mathcal{G}(A) encapsulates the first condition of Definition 6 in the sense that elements of T​𝒢​(A)T\mathcal{G}(A) vanish on functions that only depend on one variable, whereas the second condition is not accounted for.

In order to state our main result, we need the following definition:

Definition 40 (Interior points).

An operator Γ∈𝒢0​(A)\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}^{0}(A) is called an interior point, if

  1. 1.

    for all d​Γ∈T​𝒢​(A)\mathrm{d}\Gamma\in T\mathcal{G}(A) there exists C>0C>0 such that ℒ¯Γ+ε​d​Γ∈𝒢0​(A)\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}+\varepsilon\mathrm{d}\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}^{0}(A) for all ε∈(−C,C){\varepsilon\in(-C,C)},

  2. 2.

    the operator ℒ¯Γ\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma} is invertible on L02​(π¯Γ)L_{0}^{2}(\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}),

  3. 3.

    d​Γ​ℒΓ−1​f∈C⁡(E¯)\mathrm{d}\Gamma\mathcal{L}^{-1}_{\Gamma}f\in C(\bar{E}) for all d​Γ∈T​𝒢​(A)\mathrm{d}\Gamma\in T\mathcal{G}(A) and all f∈C⁡(E¯)∩L02​(π¯Γ)f\in C(\bar{E})\cap L_{0}^{2}(\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}).

Remark 41.

The first condition is the essence of the foregoing definition, describing the geometric intuition of interior points. The third condition is mostly technical, since in applications ℒΓ−1\mathcal{L}_{\Gamma}^{-1} usually possesses sufficient smoothing properties in order for the composition d​Γ​ℒΓ−1\mathrm{d}\Gamma\mathcal{L}_{\Gamma}^{-1} to preserve continuity.

Remark 42 (Lyapunov functions).

It is possible and often convenient to replace the second condition by the weaker requirement that invertibility holds on a suitable subspace 𝒱Γ\mathcal{V}_{\Gamma} of L02​(π¯Γ)L_{0}^{2}(\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}). Our results in this section will then continue to hold, provided that the cost function cc satisfies c−π¯Γ​(c)∈𝒱Γc-\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}(c)\in\mathcal{V}_{\Gamma} for all interior points Γ\Gamma. As an example, assume that there exist Lyapunov functions 𝒦i:Ei→[1,∞)\mathcal{K}_{i}:E_{i}\rightarrow[1,\infty) for the one-particle dynamics, i.e.

ℒi​𝒦i≤−ai​𝒦i+bi,\mathcal{L}_{i}\mathcal{K}_{i}\leq-a_{i}\mathcal{K}_{i}+b_{i}, (118)

for suitable constants ai>0a_{i}>0, bi≥0b_{i}\geq 0. Defining 𝒦¯=∑i=1n𝒦i\bar{\mathcal{K}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{K}_{i}, it follows immediately from Γ​𝒦¯=0\Gamma\bar{\mathcal{K}}=0 that 𝒦¯\bar{\mathcal{K}} is a Lyapunov function for ℒ¯Γ\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}, independently of the coupling operator Γ\Gamma. Under certain minorisation (irreducibility) conditions (see [38], [54, Chapter 2.4]), one can show that ℒΓ−1\mathcal{L}_{\Gamma}^{-1} is invertible on

𝒱Γ={f∈L02​(π¯Γ):‖f𝒦¯‖∞<∞}.\mathcal{V}_{\Gamma}=\left\{f\in L_{0}^{2}(\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}):\,\left\|\frac{f}{\bar{\mathcal{K}}}\right\|_{\infty}<\infty\right\}. (119)

See also [37, Theorem 3.2].

Example 43.

In the setting of Section 3.1.1 (overdamped Langevin dynamics), it is straightforward to see that Γ\Gamma as defined in (47) satisfies condition 1 of Definition 40 if and only if −1<α⁡(x,y)<1-1<\alpha(x,y)<1 for all (x,y)∈ℝ2(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, i.e. if and only if the bound (48) is strict. More generally, Γ\Gamma as defined in (58) satisfies condition 1 if and only if the matrix QQ as defined in (59) is (strictly) positive definite pointwise. Those conditions are clearly equivalent to the (pointwise) ellipticity of the corresponding generators ℒ¯Γ\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}. In the case of underdamped Langevin dynamics (Section 3.2), analogous statements are valid. Similarly, couplings of zigzag processes (Section 3.3) satisfy condition 1 if and only if the bound (91) is strictly satisfied.

For our further discussion, we will need the following derivative formula:

Proposition 44.

Let Γ∈𝒢0​(A)\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}^{0}(A) be an interior point, d​Γ∈T​𝒢​(A)\mathrm{d}\Gamma\in T\mathcal{G}(A), and consider the family of operators ℒ¯Γ+ε​d​Γ∈𝒢0\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}+\varepsilon\mathrm{d}\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}^{0}, for ε\varepsilon small enough. Let the associated family of invariant measures be denoted by π¯Γε\bar{\pi}^{\varepsilon}_{\Gamma} and fix c∈Cb​(E¯)c\in C_{b}(\bar{E}). Then the function ε↦∫E¯c​d​π¯Γε\varepsilon\mapsto\int_{\bar{E}}c\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}^{\varepsilon}_{\Gamma} is differentiable in ε=0\varepsilon=0, and the derivative is given by

dd​ε|ε=0(∫E¯cdπ¯Γε)=−∫E¯c[ℒ¯Γ∗]−1(dΓ∗𝟏)dπ¯Γ0,\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\varepsilon}\bigg\rvert_{\varepsilon=0}\left(\int_{\bar{E}}c\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}^{\varepsilon}_{\Gamma}\right)=-\int_{\bar{E}}c\left[\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}^{*}\right]^{-1}(\mathrm{d}\Gamma^{*}\mathbf{1})\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}^{0}, (120)

where the adjoints are taken in L2​(π¯Γ0)L^{2}(\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}^{0}).

Proof.

The proof can be found in Appendix B. ∎

Remark 45.

Notice that our notation entails that π¯Γ≡π¯Γ0\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}\equiv\bar{\pi}^{0}_{\Gamma}. Moreover, the right-hand side of (120) is well defined. Indeed, by the second condition in Definition 40, [ℒ¯Γ∗]−1\left[\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}^{*}\right]^{-1} is well defined on L02​(π¯Γ0)L^{2}_{0}(\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}^{0}) and furthermore Ran⁡d​Γ∗⊆L02​(π¯Γ0)\Ran\mathrm{d}\Gamma^{*}\subseteq L^{2}_{0}(\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}^{0}) due to

∫E¯d​Γ∗​f​d​π¯Γ0=∫E¯(d​Γ​𝟏)​f​d​π¯Γ0=0,f∈Cc∞​(E¯),\int_{\bar{E}}\mathrm{d}\Gamma^{*}f\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}^{0}=\int_{\bar{E}}(\mathrm{d}\Gamma\mathbf{1})f\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}^{0}=0,\quad f\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\bar{E}), (121)

using that d​Γ​𝟏=0\mathrm{d}\Gamma\mathbf{1}=0 according to Lemma 18.

For an interior point Γ∈𝒢0​(A)\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}^{0}(A) and d​Γ∈T​𝒢​(A)\mathrm{d}\Gamma\in T\mathcal{G}(A) let us introduce the suggestive notation

dd​Γ∫E¯cdπ¯Γ:=dd​ε|ε=0(∫E¯cdπ¯Γε),\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\Gamma}\int_{\bar{E}}c\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}:=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\varepsilon}\bigg\rvert_{\varepsilon=0}\left(\int_{\bar{E}}c\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}^{\varepsilon}_{\Gamma}\right), (122)

as well as the following terminology:

Definition 46 (Critical points).

Let Γ∈𝒢⁡(A)\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}(A) be an interior point. Then Γ\Gamma is called critical if

dd​Γ​∫E¯c​d​π¯Γ=0\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\Gamma}\int_{\bar{E}}c\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}=0 (123)

for all d​Γ∈T​𝒢​(A)\mathrm{d}\Gamma\in T\mathcal{G}(A).

In our aim to find minimisers of the function Γ↦∫E¯c​d​π¯Γ\Gamma\mapsto\int_{\bar{E}}c\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}, it is natural to seek critical points. The following is our main result in this section:

Theorem 47.

Let c∈Cb​(E¯)c\in C_{b}(\bar{E}). Then either all interior points are critical, or no interior point is critical.

Example 48.

Let cc be of the form

c⁡(x1,…,xn)=g1​(x1)+…+gn​(xn),c(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=g_{1}(x_{1})+\ldots+g_{n}(x_{n}), (124)

for appropriate functions gi:Ei→ℝg_{i}:E_{i}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}. Then, since π¯Γ\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma} is a coupling of the fixed marginals (πi)i=1n(\pi_{i})_{i=1}^{n}, the function Γ↦∫E¯c​d​π¯Γ=∑i=1n∫Eigi​d​πi\Gamma\mapsto\int_{\bar{E}}c\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\int_{E_{i}}g_{i}\,\mathrm{d}\pi_{i} is constant, and hence all interior points are critical.

Before proceeding to the proof of the theorem, let us give a few remarks:

Remark 49.

Informally, Theorem 47 states that the mapping 𝒢0​(A)∋Γ↦∫E¯c​d​π¯Γ\mathcal{G}^{0}(A)\ni\Gamma\mapsto\int_{\bar{E}}c\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma} is either locally constant or does not attain its extrema on interior points. In other words, if Γ↦∫E¯c​d​π¯Γ\Gamma\mapsto\int_{\bar{E}}c\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma} is not constant, then its extrema lie ‘at the boundary’ of 𝒢0​(A)\mathcal{G}^{0}(A), although we have not rigorously defined this term, and moreover, ∫E¯c​d​π¯Γ\int_{\bar{E}}c\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma} is not even well-defined for nonergodic couplings.

Remark 50.

A striking consequence of Theorem 47 is that under mild conditions, independent coupling (associated to 𝟎∈𝒢0\mathbf{0}\in\mathcal{G}^{0}) of overdamped or underdamped Langevin dynamics is not optimal for any criterion of the form ∫E¯c​d​π¯Γ\int_{\bar{E}}c\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}. Theorem 47 complements results from the theory of optimal transportation that state that optimal couplings are generically singular in terms of their support. Indeed, considering the example of overdamped or underdamped Langevin dynamics, the ‘boundary of 𝒢0​(A)\mathcal{G}^{0}(A)’ consists of couplings that lead to degenerately elliptic generators that are in general not hypoelliptic. In particular, the corresponding invariant measures are not in general absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure.

Remark 51.

Theorem 47 also supports the folklore that optimal Markov chain Monte Carlo samplers use as little noise as possible to guarantee ergodicity, as degenerately elliptic operators correspond to dynamics where noise only acts in certain directions. For example, it is by now well-documented that nonreversible samplers outperform their reversible counterparts in various settings (see for instance [27, 42, 67, 74]). The process of making a reversible sampler nonreversible can be thought of informally as decreasing the ratio between random and deterministic behaviour.

Remark 52.

Let us examine the function 𝒢0​(A)∋Γ↦∫E¯c​d​π¯Γ\mathcal{G}^{0}(A)\ni\Gamma\mapsto\int_{\bar{E}}c\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma} along a ray. More precisely, fix d​Γ∈T​𝒢​(A)\mathrm{d}\Gamma\in T\mathcal{G}(A), set ℒ¯ε:=ℒ¯0+ε​d​Γ\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\varepsilon}:=\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}+\varepsilon\mathrm{d}\Gamma for ε\varepsilon small enough, and consider the function ε↦∫E¯c​d​π¯ε\varepsilon\mapsto\int_{\bar{E}}c\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\varepsilon}, where (π¯ε)ε(\bar{\pi}_{\varepsilon})_{\varepsilon} denotes the corresponding family of invariant measures. Since d​Γ\mathrm{d}\Gamma is relatively bounded with respect to ℒ¯0\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0} in L2​(π¯0)L^{2}(\bar{\pi}_{0}), we have the following Neumann power expansion for ε\varepsilon small enough:

∫E¯c​d​π¯ε=∫E¯c⁡(1+∑j=1∞(−ε)j​[(d​Γ​ℒ¯0−1)∗]j)​𝟏​d​π¯0.\int_{\bar{E}}c\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\varepsilon}=\int_{\bar{E}}c\left(1+\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}(-\varepsilon)^{j}[(\mathrm{d}\Gamma\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{-1})^{*}]^{j}\right)\mathbf{1}\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{0}. (125)

For details, see [54, Theorem 5.2]. The factor of (−ε)j(-\varepsilon)^{j} in expression (125) signals oscillatory behaviour, and indeed it is straightforward to construct examples (for instance in the Gaussian case), where (125) exhibits multiple local minima and maxima as a function of ε\varepsilon (see for instance the graph related to linear coupling in Figure 3(c) below). This finding is not in contradiction with Theorem 47. Indeed, as Theorem 47 shows, at those extrema there are directions of ascent (or descent) in T​𝒢​(A)T\mathcal{G}(A) not aligned with the considered ray and thus, those extrema turn out not to be critical when considered in the whole of 𝒢0​(A)\mathcal{G}^{0}(A).

Let us now prove Theorem 47 and start with the following key lemma. Its significance derives from the fact that the second statement manifestly does not depend on Γ\Gamma.

Lemma 53.

Let c∈Cb​(E¯)∩L02​(π¯0)c\in C_{b}(\bar{E})\cap L_{0}^{2}(\bar{\pi}_{0}) and Γ∈𝒢0​(A)\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}^{0}(A) be an interior point. Then the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. 1.

    The following holds for all admissible indices (i,j,k,l)∈𝒥(i,j,k,l)\in\mathcal{J}:

    Aki​Alj​ℒ¯Γ−1​(c−π¯Γ​(c))=0.A_{k}^{i}A_{l}^{j}\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}^{-1}\left(c-\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}(c)\right)=0. (126)
  2. 2.

    There exists f∈𝒟⁡(ℒ¯0)f\in\mathcal{D}(\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}) such that both of the following hold:

    1. (a)

      for all admissible indices (i,j,k,l)∈𝒥(i,j,k,l)\in\mathcal{J} it holds that

      Aki​Alj​f=0,A_{k}^{i}A_{l}^{j}f=0, (127)
    2. (b)
      ℒ¯0​f=c.\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}f=c. (128)
Proof.

First assume that (126) holds for all (i,j,k,l)∈𝒥(i,j,k,l)\in\mathcal{J}. Then setting

f=ℒ¯Γ−1​(c−π¯Γ​(c))f=\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}^{-1}\left(c-\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}(c)\right)

immediately implies (127). Furthermore, from (127) and (116) it follows that ℒ¯Γ​f=ℒ¯0​f\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}f=\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}f, implying

ℒ¯0​f=(c−π¯Γ​(c)),\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}f=\left(c-\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}(c)\right), (129)

as well as f∈𝒟⁡(ℒ¯0)f\in\mathcal{D}(\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}). Equation (129) clearly implies that π¯0​(c)=π¯Γ​(c)\bar{\pi}_{0}(c)=\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}(c), and hence π¯Γ​(c)=0\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}(c)=0, leading to (128).

The reverse implication follows similarly by first observing that (127) and (128) imply that ℒ¯Γ​f=c\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}f=c, and hence π¯Γ​(c)=0\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}(c)=0. Combining this with (127) shows that (126) holds. ∎

Proof of Theorem 47.

Clearly, we can without loss of generality assume that π¯0​(c)=0\bar{\pi}_{0}(c)=0. According to Definition 46 and Proposition 44, an interior point Γ∈𝒢0​(A)\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}^{0}(A) is critical if and only if

∫E¯c​[ℒ¯Γ∗]−1​(d​Γ∗​1)​d​π¯Γ=0,\int_{\bar{E}}c\left[\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}^{*}\right]^{-1}(\mathrm{d}\Gamma^{*}1)\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}=0, (130)

for all d​Γ∈T​𝒢​(A)\mathrm{d}\Gamma\in T\mathcal{G}(A), which is equivalent to

∑(i,j,k,l)∈𝒥∫E¯(Aki​Alj​ℒ¯Γ−1​(c−π¯Γ​(c)))⋅αi​j​k​l​d​π¯Γ=0,\sum_{(i,j,k,l)\in\mathcal{J}}\int_{\bar{E}}\left(A_{k}^{i}A_{l}^{j}\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}^{-1}\left(c-\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}(c)\right)\right)\cdot\alpha_{ijkl}\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}=0, (131)

for all (αi​j​k​l)(i,j,k,l)∈𝒥⊂Cc∞​(E¯)(\alpha_{ijkl})_{(i,j,k,l)\in\mathcal{J}}\subset C_{c}^{\infty}(\bar{E}). The latter statement is clearly equivalent to the first statement in Lemma 53. The result now follows by noting that the second statement in Lemma 53 does not depend on Γ\Gamma. ∎

5 A perturbative approach for the study of the asymptotic variance

Informally speaking, Theorem 47 shows that the objective of optimising the asymptotic variance σF2\sigma_{F}^{2} leads to the requirement that Γ∈𝒢0​(A)\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}^{0}(A) should be chosen to be a ‘boundary point’ (see the discussion in Remark 49). While being an interesting theoretical result, it does not give much guidance about how to choose a suitable coupling in practice (after all, both minima and maxima are obtained ‘at the boundary’ of 𝒢0​(A)\mathcal{G}^{0}(A)). In this section we therefore develop a perturbative approach, based on operators of the form

ℒ¯Γε=ℒ¯0+ε​d​Γ,d​Γ∈T​𝒢​(A),\bar{\mathcal{L}}^{\varepsilon}_{\Gamma}=\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}+\varepsilon\mathrm{d}\Gamma,\quad\mathrm{d}\Gamma\in T\mathcal{G}(A), (132)

for ε\varepsilon small enough. In the following, we will assume that ε∈ℐ\varepsilon\in\mathcal{I}, where ℐ⊂ℝ\mathcal{I}\subset\mathbb{R} is an appropriate interval such that ℒ¯Γε∈𝒢0\bar{\mathcal{L}}^{\varepsilon}_{\Gamma}\in\mathcal{G}^{0} for all ε∈ℐ\varepsilon\in\mathcal{I}. As usual, we consider observables of the form F=1n​∑i=1nfiF=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}, for some fi∈L02​(πi)f_{i}\in L_{0}^{2}(\pi_{i}), and suppose that Assumption 3 is satisfied. To stress the dependence of the asymptotic variance on the parameter ε\varepsilon we will write σF2​(ε)\sigma_{F}^{2}(\varepsilon). Note that a similar setting has already been considered in Remark 52. There, we investigated the dependence of the asymptotic variance (or more generally, of the quantity ∫E¯c​d​π¯ε\int_{\bar{E}}c\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\varepsilon}) on the parameter ε\varepsilon. Here, we are rather interested in the choice of the ‘direction’ d​Γ∈T​𝒢​(A)\mathrm{d}\Gamma\in T\mathcal{G}(A), starting from the trivial (independent) coupling ℒ¯0\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}.

Combining the expression (97) with either (125) or (120) we see that

dd​ε​σF2|ε=0=∫E¯d​Γ​ξ​d​π¯0,\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\varepsilon}\sigma_{F}^{2}\big|_{\varepsilon=0}=\int_{\bar{E}}\mathrm{d}\Gamma\xi\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{0}, (133)

where ξ\xi is given by

ξ=1n2​∑i<jϕi​ϕj,\xi=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i<j}\phi_{i}\phi_{j}, (134)

in terms of the solutions to the Poisson equations (92). The benefit of (133) is that its right-hand side consists of expressions that are known in principle, as the measure π¯0\bar{\pi}_{0} is given by the product π¯0=⨂i=1nπi\bar{\pi}_{0}=\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n}\pi_{i}. It therefore serves as a starting point for finding a suitable coupling operator Γ∈𝒢\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}. Let us summarise our approach in this section in the following form:

Problem 2.

Given invariant measures πi∈𝒫⁡(Ei)\pi_{i}\in\mathcal{P}(E_{i}) and observables fi∈L02​(πi)f_{i}\in L_{0}^{2}(\pi_{i}), find a coupling operator Γ∈𝒢\Gamma\in\mathcal{G} such that

∫E¯Γ​ξ​d​π¯0\int_{\bar{E}}\Gamma\xi\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{0} (135)

is minimised.

Problem 2 can be thought of in two different ways: Firstly, it can be interpreted as a linearisation of Problem 1. Indeed, (135) depends linearly on Γ\Gamma, whereas (108) is highly nonlinear (for an illustration of this fact, see the power expansion (125)). Another way of seeing this is by noting the similarity between (135) and the second term appearing on the right-hand side of (101). Not surprisingly, Problem 2 turns out to be much easier to (approximately) solve in practice. Note that by linearity, properties similar to the one expressed in Theorem 47 hold for Problem 2 (at least if 𝒢\mathcal{G} is convex). Choosing a coupling Γ∈𝒢\Gamma\in\mathcal{G} according to the formulation of Problem 2 is clearly heuristic. However, we have had good results with it in numerical experiments (see below).

Secondly, when a solution of Problem 2 is available, it is reasonable in practice to only implement a small perturbation of the independent sampler (i.e. choose ε\varepsilon to be small). Such a choice will not be optimal over all couplings in 𝒢\mathcal{G} according to Theorem 47. However, it is then guaranteed that the performance of the sampler is at least slightly improved. Let us also note that the formulation of Problem 2 does not require the coupling to be ergodic, as opposed to the formulation of Problem 1.

The aim of this section is to analyse Problem 2 for some of the examples presented in Chapter 3 and to present some numerical experiments. To this end, let us introduce the shorthand notation

δ​σF2​(Γ):=∫E¯Γ​ξ​d​π¯0,\delta\sigma_{F}^{2}(\Gamma):=\int_{\bar{E}}\Gamma\xi\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{0}, (136)

stressing the infinitesimal (approximate) nature of the objective in Problem 2. In the sequel, Γ\Gamma will be given in terms of a function α\alpha, belonging to a set 𝒜\mathcal{A}. To emphasize this dependence we will write Γα\Gamma_{\alpha}. We will not impose regularity constraints on the function α\alpha (beyond measurability), so that the operators Γα\Gamma_{\alpha} will in general not induce couplings that satisfy the Feller property (see Remark 21) and hence strictly speaking do not belong to 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

5.1 Overdamped Langevin dynamics in one dimension with two particles

Consider the setting from the example presented in Section 3.1.1. Then, (136) takes the form

δ​σF2​(Γα)=∫ℝ2α⁡(x,y)​ϕ′​(x)​ϕ′​(y)​e−(V⁡(x)+V⁡(y))​𝑑x​𝑑y,\delta\sigma_{F}^{2}(\Gamma_{\alpha})=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\alpha(x,y)\phi^{\prime}(x)\phi^{\prime}(y)e^{-\left(V(x)+V(y)\right)}\,\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}y, (137)

where ϕ\phi is the solution to the Poisson equation

−(−V′​ϕ′+ϕ′′)=f,π⁡(ϕ)=0,-\left(-V^{\prime}\phi^{\prime}+\phi^{\prime\prime}\right)=f,\quad\pi(\phi)=0, (138)

and f∈L02​(π)f\in L_{0}^{2}(\pi) is an observable of interest. Furthermore, Γ\Gamma is given as in (47), with

α∈𝒜:={α:ℝ2→ℝ|αmeasurable, −1≤α≤1}.\alpha\in\mathcal{A}:=\{\alpha:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\,|\,\alpha\,\text{measurable, }-1\leq\alpha\leq 1\}. (139)

Recall from Section 3.1.1 that α∈𝒜\alpha\in\mathcal{A} induces a well-defined coupled process (Lemma 22) that however does not satisfy the Feller property in general (further regularity assumptions would be required). The following optimality result is immediate from an inspection of (137):

Proposition 54.

Let α∗∈𝒜\alpha^{*}\in\mathcal{A} be given by

α∗​(x,y)={1if ​ϕ′​(x)​ϕ′​(y)≤0,−1if ​ϕ′​(x)​ϕ′​(y)>0,\alpha^{*}(x,y)=\begin{cases}1\quad&\mbox{if }\;\phi^{\prime}(x)\phi^{\prime}(y)\leq 0,\\ -1\quad&\mbox{if }\;\phi^{\prime}(x)\phi^{\prime}(y)>0,\\ \end{cases} (140)

Then Γα∗\Gamma_{\alpha^{*}} solves Problem 2 in the sense that δ​σF2​(Γα∗)≤δ​σF2​(Γα)\delta\sigma_{F}^{2}(\Gamma_{\alpha^{*}})\leq\delta\sigma_{F}^{2}(\Gamma_{\alpha}) for all α∈𝒜\alpha\in\mathcal{A}.

Remark 55.

Clearly, we have

∫E¯Γα∗​ξ​d​π¯Γ≤0,\int_{\bar{E}}\Gamma_{\alpha^{*}}\xi\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}\leq 0, (141)

for α∗\alpha^{*} as defined in (140). We stress the difference between this expression and (137), where we compute the same integral, but with respect to π¯0\bar{\pi}_{0}. By comparison with (101), we see that σF2​(Γα∗)≤σF2​(𝟎)\sigma_{F}^{2}(\Gamma_{\alpha^{*}})\leq\sigma_{F}^{2}(\mathbf{0}), i.e. Γα∗\Gamma_{\alpha^{*}} always improves on independent coupling. However, we do not know whether Γα∗\Gamma_{\alpha^{*}} is optimal in the sense of Problem 1.

It is instructive to compare the solution of Problem 2 found in Proposition 54 to the solution of the usual Kantorovich problem. Recall that Problem 2 can be considered to be a linearisation of Problem 1, which in turn is related to the Kantorovich problem in the sense that the minimisation is carried out over a smaller set of couplings (namely those couplings that are invariant measures of coupled processes, see Definition 35). For our experiments, we choose the quadratic potential V⁡(x)=12​x2V(x)=\frac{1}{2}x^{2}, i.e. the task of sampling from a Gaussian measure. Furthermore, we consider the linear observable f1​(x)=xf_{1}(x)=x, the quadratic observable f2​(x)=x2f_{2}(x)=x^{2} and the ‘mixed’ observable f3​(x)=x2−xf_{3}(x)=x^{2}-x. In Figure 2(c), we plot the invariant measure of the coupled processes induced by (140) (left-hand side) and compare them to the solutions of the Kantorovich problem99 9 The optimal transport map was computed using the Python library POT 0.4.0 (accessible from https://pypi.python.org/pypi/POT/0.4.0) which is based on the algorithm proposed in [12]. (right-hand side), with the appropriate cost function c=−ℒ¯0​ξc=-\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}\xi as given in Section 4.2. As it turns out, the solutions to Problem 2 and the standard Kantorovich problem look remarkably similar (at least in shape). We hence conclude that in the example considered here, Problem 2 is a good approximation of Problem 1, keeping in mind that the solution of the Kantorovich problem provides a lower bound for the objective function of Problem 1 (see Remark 37).

The following lemma serves to examine a few test cases and gain further intuition. For convenience, let us assume that ff (and therefore, by elliptic regularity ϕ\phi) are smooth.

Lemma 56.

Let ϕ∈L02​(π)\phi\in L_{0}^{2}(\pi) solve the Poisson equation (138).

  1. 1.

    Assume that f∈L02​(π)f\in L_{0}^{2}(\pi) is monotonically increasing (decreasing). Then ϕ′\phi^{\prime} is nonnegative (nonpositive).

  2. 2.

    Assume that VV and ff are symmetric, i.e. V⁡(−x)=V⁡(x)V(-x)=V(x) and f⁡(−x)=f⁡(x)f(-x)=f(x) for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. Furthermore, let ff be monotonically decreasing (increasing) on (−∞,0](-\infty,0]. Then ϕ′​(x)⋅x≤0\phi^{\prime}(x)\cdot x\leq 0 (ϕ′​(x)⋅x≥0\phi^{\prime}(x)\cdot x\geq 0) for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}.

The proof can be found in Appendix C. The following two corollaries are direct consequences of Lemma 56 and Proposition 54:

Corollary 57 (‘Mirror coupling’).

In the setting from the first part of Lemma 56,

α∗≡−1\alpha^{*}\equiv-1

solves Problem 2, in the sense that δ​σF2​(Γα∗)≤δ​σF2​(Γα)\delta\sigma_{F}^{2}(\Gamma_{\alpha^{*}})\leq\delta\sigma_{F}^{2}(\Gamma_{\alpha}) for all α∈𝒜\alpha\in\mathcal{A}.

Corollary 58 (‘Symmetric coupling’).

In the setting from the second part of Lemma 56,

α∗​(x,y)={1if ​x⋅y≤0,−1if ​x⋅y>0,\alpha^{*}(x,y)=\begin{cases}1\quad&\mbox{if }x\cdot y\leq 0,\\ -1\quad&\mbox{if }x\cdot y>0,\\ \end{cases} (142)

solves Problem 2, in the sense that δ​σF2​(Γα∗)≤δ​σF2​(Γα)\delta\sigma_{F}^{2}(\Gamma_{\alpha^{*}})\leq\delta\sigma_{F}^{2}(\Gamma_{\alpha}) for all α∈𝒜\alpha\in\mathcal{A}.

A few comments on the findings from Corollaries 57 and 58 are in order. If the observable is monotone (Corollary 57), then it turns out that choosing the ‘mirror coupling’ d​Btx=−d​Bty\mathrm{d}B_{t}^{x}=-\mathrm{d}B_{t}^{y} in (53) is optimal in the sense of Problem 2. This result has a clear connection to popular variance reduction techniques such as ‘antithetic variates’ [47, Chapter 9.2], where correlations between random variables are used to produce cancellations. In the case of symmetric observables (Corollary 58), optimal coupling in the sense of Problem 2 leads to a more sophisticated strategy: When the two particles (the locations of which are again denoted by xx and yy) ‘are on the same side of the potential’ (meaning that x≥0x\geq 0 and y≥0y\geq 0 or x≤0x\leq 0 and y≤0y\leq 0), then the Brownian motions should be coupled according to d​Btx=−d​Bty\mathrm{d}B_{t}^{x}=-\mathrm{d}B_{t}^{y}, as in the case of monotone observables. When the particles are on opposite sides (x≥0x\geq 0 and y≤0y\leq 0 or x≤0x\leq 0 and y≥0y\geq 0), according to Corollary 58 it is best to switch to ‘synchronous coupling’, d​Btx=d​Bty\mathrm{d}B_{t}^{x}=\mathrm{d}B_{t}^{y}. Intuitively this can be understood as follows: By symmetry, the situation where x≥0x\geq 0 and y≤0y\leq 0 with synchronous coupling (d​Btx=d​Bty\mathrm{d}B_{t}^{x}=\mathrm{d}B_{t}^{y}) is equivalent to x≥0x\geq 0 and y≥0y\geq 0, with mirror coupling (d​Btx=−d​Bty\mathrm{d}B_{t}^{x}=-\mathrm{d}B_{t}^{y}). Since ff is monotone on [0,∞)[0,\infty), this argument provides a plausible explanation for optimality by appealing to Corollary 57. Finally, let us mention that numerical experiments show that using mirror coupling in the case of observables of the type encountered in Corollary 58 (‘naive antithetic variates’) actually leads to a less effective sampler in terms of the asymptotic variance (see Figure 3(b)).

Let us consider now the same set-up as in the numerical experiments presented in Figure 2(c), i.e. we consider a Gaussian target measure (V⁡(x)=12​x2V(x)=\frac{1}{2}x^{2}), and the observables f1​(x)=xf_{1}(x)=x (‘linear’), f2​(x)=x2f_{2}(x)=x^{2} (‘quadratic’) and f3​(x)=x2−xf_{3}(x)=x^{2}-x (‘mixed’). In Figure 3, we plot the asymptotic variances for f1f_{1}, f2f_{2} and f3f_{3}, associated to different coupling schemes as a function of the coupling strength β\beta. To be precise, the ‘Poisson’ coupling is defined by

α⁡(x,y)={2​sin⁡β​cos⁡βif ​ϕ′​(x)​ϕ′​(y)≤0,−2​sin⁡β​cos⁡βif ​ϕ′​(x)​ϕ′​(y)>0,\alpha(x,y)=\begin{cases}2\sin\beta\cos\beta\quad&\mbox{if }\;\phi^{\prime}(x)\phi^{\prime}(y)\leq 0,\\ -2\sin\beta\cos\beta\quad&\mbox{if }\;\phi^{\prime}(x)\phi^{\prime}(y)>0,\\ \end{cases} (143)

ϕ\phi being the solution to the Poisson equation (138) for the corresponding observable, and β∈[0,π4]\beta\in[0,\frac{\pi}{4}] denoting the coupling strength1010 10 For β∈[0,π4]\beta\in[0,\frac{\pi}{4}], the function 2sinβcos2\sin\beta\cos is monotone, taking values in [0,1][0,1]. We chose this parametrisation in order for it to be consistent with (52).. For β=0\beta=0, we recover independent coupling, whereas β=π4\beta=\frac{\pi}{4} leads to the optimal coupling from Proposition 54. According to Corollaries 57 and 58, Poisson coupling coincides with mirror coupling for f1f_{1} and with symmetric coupling for f2f_{2}. To illustrate the effect of couplings that are not tailored to the observable of interest, we also plot the asymptotic variances associated to symmetric coupling for f1f_{1}, mirror coupling for f2f_{2}, and both mirror and symmetric coupling for f3f_{3}. For f3f_{3}, we furthermore consider a coupling strategy that uses the derivative of the observable instead of the derivative of the solution to the Poisson equation, specifically, the coupling induced by

α⁡(x,y)={2​sin⁡β​cos⁡βif ​f′​(x)​f′​(y)≤0,−2​sin⁡β​cos⁡βif ​f′​(x)​f′​(y)>0.\alpha(x,y)=\begin{cases}2\sin\beta\cos\beta\quad&\mbox{if }\;f^{\prime}(x)f^{\prime}(y)\leq 0,\\ -2\sin\beta\cos\beta\quad&\mbox{if }\;f^{\prime}(x)f^{\prime}(y)>0.\\ \end{cases} (144)

The motivation for this is that in applications, the solution to the Poisson equation is often hard to obtain1111 11 However, often one aims to approximate the solution to the Poisson equation in order to use it as a control variate, see for instance [26, 62, 76]. It suggests itself to use those approaches in conjunction with the coupling strategy developed here., whereas the gradient of the observable is readily available. By integration by parts we have

∫ℝd∇f⋅∇ϕ​𝑑π=∫ℝdf2​𝑑π≥0,\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\nabla f\cdot\nabla\phi\,\mathrm{d}\pi=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}f^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\pi\geq 0, (145)

suggesting us to use ∇f\nabla f as a surrogate for ∇ϕ\nabla\phi (at equilibrium, the scalar product of ∇f\nabla f and ∇ϕ\nabla\phi is positive on average).

In all the cases considered, the Poisson coupling turns out be the most efficient, uniformly in the coupling strength β\beta. The fact that the absolute value of the derivative d​σF2d​β|β=0\frac{\mathrm{d}\sigma_{F}^{2}}{\mathrm{d}\beta}|_{\beta=0} is maximal for Poisson coupling is precisely the content of Proposition 54, whereas the fact that the asymptotic variance for Poisson coupling is maximal at β=0\beta=0 follows from Remark 55. It is interesting to note the monotonity of the asymptotic variance associated to Poisson coupling with respect to the coupling strength β\beta; this phenomenon is not covered by our theory. Importantly, the efficiency of a certain coupling strongly depends on the considered observable. Indeed, the mirror coupling (which is excellent for the linear observable, see Figure 3(a)) leads to an increase of the asymptotic variance for the quadratic observable (see Figure 3(b)). Similarly, the symmetric coupling (suited for the quadratic observable), does not improve the performance for the linear observable (but the performance is also not worsened). In Figure 3(c), we observe that the coupling based on the derivative of the observable (see (144)) works almost as well as the Poisson coupling, so this might be a reasonable choice in applications, although further studies are needed. For a comment about the minimum of the graph associated to mirror coupling for the mixed observable (see Figure 3(c)) we refer to Remark 52.

5.2 Overdamped Langevin dynamics with multiple particles in arbitrary dimensions

Let us extend the discussion from the previous section to arbitrary dimensions, first considering the case of two particles (as done in Example 28). Using the expression (68), we see that

δσF2(Γα)=∫ℝd×ℝd(∇ϕ(y)⋅α(x,y)∇ϕ(x))e−(V⁡(x)+V⁡(y))dxdy,\delta\sigma_{F}^{2}(\Gamma_{\alpha})=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left(\nabla\phi(y)\cdot\alpha(x,y)\nabla\phi(x)\right)e^{-(V(x)+V(y))}\,\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}y, (146)

where α:ℝd×ℝd→ℝd×d\alpha:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} is a matrix-valued function satisfying (67), i.e.

α∈𝒜:={α:ℝd×ℝd→ℝd×dmeasurable, α(x,y)Tα(x,y)≤Id×dfor all x,y∈ℝd},\alpha\in\mathcal{A}:=\left\{\alpha:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\;\,\text{measurable, }\alpha(x,y)^{T}\alpha(x,y)\leq I_{d\times d}\;\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\right\}, (147)

and ϕ\phi is the solution to the Poisson equation

−(−∇V⋅∇+Δ)ϕ=f,π(ϕ)=0.-(-\nabla V\cdot\nabla+\Delta)\phi=f,\quad\pi(\phi)=0. (148)

Since (67) implies

we get the following optimality result:

Proposition 59.

Assume that α∗∈𝒜\alpha^{*}\in\mathcal{A} is chosen such that

∇ϕ(y)⋅α∗(x,y)∇ϕ(x)=−|∇ϕ(x)||∇ϕ(y)|,x,y∈ℝd.\nabla\phi(y)\cdot\alpha^{*}(x,y)\nabla\phi(x)=-|\nabla\phi(x)||\nabla\phi(y)|,\quad x,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. (150)

Then α∗\alpha^{*} solves Problem 2, i.e. δ​σF2​(Γα∗)≤δ​σF2​(Γα)\delta\sigma_{F}^{2}(\Gamma_{\alpha^{*}})\leq\delta\sigma_{F}^{2}(\Gamma_{\alpha}) for all α∈𝒜\alpha\in\mathcal{A}.

In the case when the solution ϕ\phi to the Poisson equation is known it is straightforward to construct a matrix-valued function α∗\alpha^{*} such that both (67) and (150) are satisfied. For instance, any orthogonal matrix trivially satisfies (67), and (150) can be dealt with by choosing an appropriate rotation or reflection. As an example let us mention the following reflection in the plane spanned by ∇ϕ​(x)\nabla\phi(x) and ∇ϕ​(y)\nabla\phi(y):

α∗​(x,y)={Id×d−2​(∇ϕ​(x)^+∇ϕ​(y)^)​(∇ϕ​(x)^+∇ϕ​(y)^)T(∇ϕ​(x)^+∇ϕ​(y)^)2if ∇ϕ(x)≠0,∇ϕ(y)≠0,∇ϕ​(x)^+∇ϕ​(y)^≠0,Id×dotherwise.\alpha^{*}(x,y)=\begin{cases}I_{d\times d}-2\frac{\left(\widehat{\nabla\phi(x)}+\widehat{\nabla\phi(y)}\right)\left(\widehat{\nabla\phi(x)}+\widehat{\nabla\phi(y)}\right)^{T}}{\left(\widehat{\nabla\phi(x)}+\widehat{\nabla\phi(y)}\right)^{2}}\,&\text{if }\nabla\phi(x)\neq 0,\nabla\phi(y)\neq 0,\\ &\hskip 10.0pt\widehat{\nabla\phi(x)}+\widehat{\nabla\phi(y)}\neq 0,\\ I_{d\times d}&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} (151)

Here, ∇ϕ^=∇ϕ|∇ϕ|\widehat{\nabla\phi}=\frac{\nabla\phi}{|\nabla\phi|} is used to denote the normalised gradient of ϕ\phi. As mentioned in Section 5.1, the solution to the Poisson equation is usually hard to obtain in applications (but the popular methodology using control variates relies on approximations thereof). Inspired by the integration by parts formula (145), it seems reasonable to use the normalised gradient of the observable ∇f^\widehat{\nabla f} as a surrogate for ∇ϕ^\widehat{\nabla\phi}, i.e.

αf​(x,y)={Id×d−2​(∇f​(x)^+∇f​(y)^)​(∇f​(x)^+∇f​(y)^)T(∇f​(x)^+∇f​(y)^)2if ∇f(x)≠0,∇f(y)≠0,∇f​(x)^+∇f​(y)^≠0,Id×dotherwise.\alpha_{f}(x,y)=\begin{cases}I_{d\times d}-2\frac{\left(\widehat{\nabla f(x)}+\widehat{\nabla f(y)}\right)\left(\widehat{\nabla f(x)}+\widehat{\nabla f(y)}\right)^{T}}{\left(\widehat{\nabla f(x)}+\widehat{\nabla f(y)}\right)^{2}}\,&\text{if }\nabla f(x)\neq 0,\nabla f(y)\neq 0,\\ &\hskip 10.0pt\widehat{\nabla f(x)}+\widehat{\nabla f(y)}\neq 0,\\ I_{d\times d}&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} (152)

We recall that a comparison of the couplings associated to (151) and (152) was performed in the one-dimensional case (see Figure 3(c)) where αf\alpha_{f} almost achieved the same reduction of the asymptotic variance as α∗\alpha^{*}. Based on (145) and numerical experiments we conjecture that choosing αf\alpha_{f} guarantees an improvement in terms of the asymptotic variance for small perturbations:

Conjecture 60.

Let f∈L02​(π)f\in L_{0}^{2}(\pi) and ϕ∈L02​(π)\phi\in L_{0}^{2}(\pi) be the corresponding solution to the Poisson equation (148). Then

δσF2(Γα)=∫ℝd×ℝd(∇ϕ(y)⋅αf(x,y)∇ϕ(x))e−(V⁡(x)+V⁡(y))dxdy≤0.\delta\sigma_{F}^{2}(\Gamma_{\alpha})=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left(\nabla\phi(y)\cdot\alpha_{f}(x,y)\nabla\phi(x)\right)e^{-(V(x)+V(y))}\,\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}y\leq 0. (153)

The complexity of the foregoing optimisation problems is increased substantially when considering more than two particles. From a practical perspective, it is desirable to specify the coupling in terms of the matrix-valued function GG appearing in (64) since this formulation is needed for the implementation of the numerical scheme. The linearised optimisation objective (Problem 2) however is formulated in terms of the coupling operator Γ\Gamma. Passing from the latter to GG involves the computationally expensive task of computing the square root of the matrix QQ defined in (59). The construction and effective implementation of optimally coupled samplers with multiple particles therefore remains a subject for future work, but could be based on the results for the case of two particles. To give an impression, let us outline an idea based on the notation introduced in Remark 24. It is natural to choose the orthogonal matrices gi​jg_{ij} describing the coupling between the iith and the jjth particle according to (151), i.e.

gi​j​(x1,…,xn)={Id×d−2​(∇ϕ​(xi)^+∇ϕ​(xj)^)​(∇ϕ​(xi)^+∇ϕ​(xj)^)T(∇ϕ​(xi)^+∇ϕ​(xj)^)2if ∇ϕ(xi)≠0,∇ϕ(xj)≠0,∇ϕ​(xi)^+∇ϕ​(xj)^≠0,Id×dotherwise,g_{ij}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=\begin{cases}I_{d\times d}-2\frac{\left(\widehat{\nabla\phi(x_{i})}+\widehat{\nabla\phi(x_{j})}\right)\left(\widehat{\nabla\phi(x_{i})}+\widehat{\nabla\phi(x_{j})}\right)^{T}}{\left(\widehat{\nabla\phi(x_{i})}+\widehat{\nabla\phi(x_{j})}\right)^{2}}\,&\text{if }\nabla\phi(x_{i})\neq 0,\nabla\phi(x_{j})\neq 0,\\ &\hskip 10.0pt\widehat{\nabla\phi(x_{i})}+\widehat{\nabla\phi(x_{j})}\neq 0,\\ I_{d\times d}&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases} (154)

or, when the solution ϕ\phi to the Poisson equation (or an approximation thereof) is not available, according to (152). Since the benefit of the coupling in terms of reducing the asymptotic variance is directly related to the value of the expression in (150), it is plausible to choose the weights wi​jw_{ij} (see (63)) in such a way that particle xix_{i} is preferentially coupled to particle xjx_{j} if |∇ϕ​(xi)||\nabla\phi(x_{i})| and |∇ϕ​(xj)||\nabla\phi(x_{j})| are similar in magnitude. To make this precise, denote by σ:{1,…,n}→{1,…,n}\sigma:\{1,\ldots,n\}\rightarrow\{1,\ldots,n\} the permutation that orders the particles according to |∇ϕ||\nabla\phi|, i.e.

|∇ϕ​(xσ⁡(1))|≥|∇ϕ​(xσ⁡(2))|≥…≥|∇ϕ​(xσ⁡(n−1))|≥|∇ϕ​(xσ⁡(n))|.|\nabla\phi(x_{\sigma(1)})|\geq|\nabla\phi(x_{\sigma(2)})|\geq\ldots\geq|\nabla\phi(x_{\sigma(n-1)})|\geq|\nabla\phi(x_{\sigma(n)})|. (155)

Then, denoting the coupling strength by β∈[0,π4]\beta\in[0,\frac{\pi}{4}], we can set the weights as follows:

wi​i=cosβ,i=1,…,n,\displaystyle w_{ii}=\cos\beta,\quad\quad i=1,\ldots,n,
wσ⁡(1)​σ​(2)=sin⁡β,\displaystyle w_{\sigma(1)\sigma(2)}=\sin\beta,\quad wσ⁡(3)​σ​(4)=sin⁡β,…wσ⁡(n−1)​σ​(n)=sin⁡β,\displaystyle w_{\sigma(3)\sigma(4)}=\sin\beta,\quad\ldots\quad w_{\sigma(n-1)\sigma(n)}=\sin\beta, (156)
wi​j=0otherwise.\displaystyle w_{ij}=0\quad\text{otherwise.}

Let us emphasize that the sorting of the particles according to |∇ϕ||\nabla\phi| is supposed to be performed at every time step. We have compared this coupling strategy to simple pairwise coupling without sorting1212 12 This is equivalent to running n/2n/2 two-particle samplers independently in parallel., i.e. replacing the second line of (156) by

w12=sinβ,w34=sinβ,…wn−1,n=sinβ,w_{12}=\sin\beta,\quad w_{34}=\sin\beta,\quad\ldots\quad w_{n-1,n}=\sin\beta, (157)

for the example of sampling a standard Gaussian measure (V=12​|x|2V=\frac{1}{2}|x|^{2}) in d=10d=10 dimensions with n=10n=10 particles for the quadratic observable f1​(x)=12​|x|2f_{1}(x)=\frac{1}{2}|x|^{2} and the mixed observable f2​(x)=5​|x|2+l⋅xf_{2}(x)=5|x|^{2}+l\cdot x, where l=(1,…,1)l=(1,\ldots,1). As Figure 4 shows, the sorting strategy as detailed in (156) leads to a smaller asymptotic variance in comparison to simple pairwise couplings.

5.3 The zigzag process

Recall the setting from Section 3.3 and fix an observable of interest f∈L02​(π~)f\in L_{0}^{2}(\tilde{\pi}) 1313 13 We use the notation π~​(d​x)=1Z​e−V⁡(x)​d​x\tilde{\pi}(\mathrm{d}x)=\frac{1}{Z}e^{-V(x)}\mathrm{d}x to distinguish it from the invariant measure π\pi on the full space ℝ×{−1,1}\mathbb{R}\times\{-1,1\}, given in (82).. Combining Lemma 56 with Proposition 63 immediately yields the following corollaries:

Corollary 65.

In the setting from the first part of Lemma 56,

α∗​(x,y,θx,θy)={min(λ(x,θx),λ(y,θy)),if ​θx​θy≤00,otherwise,\alpha^{*}(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y})=\begin{cases}\min\left(\lambda(x,\theta_{x}),\lambda(y,\theta_{y})\right),\quad&\mbox{if }\theta_{x}\theta_{y}\leq 0\\ 0,\quad&\mbox{otherwise,}\end{cases} (162)

solves Problem 2, in the sense that δ​σF2​(Γα∗)≤δ​σF2​(Γα)\delta\sigma_{F}^{2}(\Gamma_{\alpha^{*}})\leq\delta\sigma_{F}^{2}(\Gamma_{\alpha}) for all α∈𝒜\alpha\in\mathcal{A}.

Corollary 66.

In the setting from the second part of Lemma 56,

α∗​(x,y,θx,θy)={min(λ(x,θx),λ(y,θy)),if ​x​y​θx​θy≤00,otherwise, \alpha^{*}(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y})=\begin{cases}\min\left(\lambda(x,\theta_{x}),\lambda(y,\theta_{y})\right),\quad&\mbox{if }xy\theta_{x}\theta_{y}\leq 0\\ 0,\quad&\mbox{otherwise, }\\ \end{cases} (163)

solves Problem 2, in the sense that δ​σF2​(Γα∗)≤δ​σF2​(Γα)\delta\sigma_{F}^{2}(\Gamma_{\alpha^{*}})\leq\delta\sigma_{F}^{2}(\Gamma_{\alpha}) for all α∈𝒜\alpha\in\mathcal{A}.

The results from Corollaries 65 and 66 can be interpreted intuitively in the following way. As already pointed out in Section 3.3, setting α⁡(x,y,θx,θy)=min⁡(λ⁡(x,θx),λ⁡(y,θy))\alpha(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y})=\min\left(\lambda(x,\theta_{x}),\lambda(y,\theta_{y})\right) encourages simultaneous flips of the velocities θx\theta_{x} and θy\theta_{y} (when the particles are at locations xx and yy, with velocities θx\theta_{x} and θy\theta_{y}), whereas the flips occur independently if α⁡(x,y,θx,θy)=0\alpha(x,y,\theta_{x},\theta_{y})=0. The coupling associated to (162) therefore leads to an increased probability of simultaneous flips precisely when the two particles move in opposite directions. Observe that simultaneous flips preserve the value of θx​θy\theta_{x}\theta_{y}, while single flips change its sign. As a consequence, the relative amount of time during which the two particles move in opposite directions is increased by the coupling associated to (162). Similarly to the case of mirror coupling for overdamped Langevin diffusions (see the discussion following Corollary 58), it is plausible that this dynamics leads to cancellations for monotone observables in the spirit of antithetic variates. The interpretation of Corollary 66 is analogous to the one of Corollary 58. For illustration, we consider again the case of a quadratic potential V⁡(x)=12​x2V(x)=\frac{1}{2}x^{2} (i.e. a Gaussian target measure) and a linear observable f⁡(x)=xf(x)=x. The coupling is chosen according to Corollary 65, i.e. in a suitable manner for the linear observable, modulated by a parameter β∈[0,1]\beta\in[0,1], analogously to (143) and (144). In Figures 5(a), 5(b), and 5(c) we plot the associated asymptotic variance, the relative time the particles move in opposite directions, as well as the average distance between the particles. Those graphs support the foregoing intuitive arguments. The fact that the average distance between the particles increases with the strength of the coupling is interesting, since it suggests that the state space can be explored more efficiently by using appropriate couplings. In Figure 5(d) we plot a typical trajectory of the joint system. Comparing this graph with the optimal transport map depicted in 2(c), we conclude that the solution to Problem 2 found in Proposition 63 is somewhat close to the solution of the Kantorovich problem, but not nearly as much as the corresponding solution in the case of overdamped Langevin dynamics. Interestingly, the aforementioned similarity is much more pronounced in the case when the target distribution is heavy-tailed. As an example, we plotted a typical trajectory of a mirror-coupled zigzag process targeting a Cauchy distribution in Figure 5(e). We did perform numerical experiments for quadratic observables. For them, an improvement in the asymptotic variance is hardly noticeable. Furthermore, a typical trajectory for the coupling induced by (163) very much resembles the typical trajectories for the independent coupling. As it seems, couplings of zigzag processes are not very efficient in the setting of Lemma 56.2. A possible explanation is that piecewise deterministic Markov processes are more ‘rigid’ than diffusions (in fact, by definition, they move deterministically during a considerable time span), allowing less flexibility in terms of couplings.

6 A remark on the rate of convergence to equilibrium

In this section, we study the rate of convergence to equilibrium for coupled processes. For convenience, let us assume that the spaces EiE_{i} and the operators ℒi\mathcal{L}_{i} are identical copies of each other. When addressing the marginal process(es), we will usually suppress the indices and write ℒ\mathcal{L} and EE. Furthermore, let us fix an ergodic coupling operator Γ∈𝒢0\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}^{0} and denote as usual the corresponding generator and semigroup by ℒ¯Γ=ℒ¯0+Γ\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{\Gamma}=\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{0}+\Gamma and (S¯tΓ)t≥0(\bar{S}^{\Gamma}_{t})_{t\geq 0} respectively. In the sequel, we will make use of the following subspace of centred observables in L02​(π¯Γ)L_{0}^{2}(\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}):

(164)

Clearly, the space L~02​(π¯Γ)\tilde{L}_{0}^{2}(\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}) comprises the observables of interest in our framework. Theorem 67.

For Λ>0\Lambda>0, the following are equivalent:

Proof of Theorem 67.

The proof is verbatim the same as for the usual result. where the last inequality uses the fact that S¯tΓ​f∈L~02​(π¯Γ)\bar{S}^{\Gamma}_{t}f\in\tilde{L}_{0}^{2}(\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}) according to Lemma 69. To explain the significance of Theorem 67, let us start by writing (165) in the form

Another short calculation shows that ℒℋ\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{H}} is symmetric with respect to \llangle⋅,⋅\rrangle\llangle\cdot,\cdot\rrangle, i.e.

If the first eigenfunction e1e_{1} is odd1414 14 In one dimension, it can be proved that the first eigenfunction is always odd by appealing to the node theorem for Schrödinger operators in Sturm-Liouville theory [81, Chapter 9]. Using (182), we hence conclude that

c1​⟨f,f⟩L2​(π)≤\llangle​f,f​\rrangle≤c2​⟨f,f⟩L2​(π),f∈L2​(π).c_{1}\langle f,f\rangle_{L^{2}(\pi)}\leq\llangle f,f\rrangle\leq c_{2}\langle f,f\rangle_{L^{2}(\pi)},\quad f\in L^{2}(\pi). (183)

By assumption, the marginal process satisfies a Poincaré inequality as well as the equivalent decay estimate

‖St​f‖L2​(π)2≤e−2​λ​t​‖f‖L2​(π)2,f∈L02​(π),\|S_{t}f\|_{L^{2}(\pi)}^{2}\leq e^{-2\lambda t}\|f\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\pi)},\quad f\in L_{0}^{2}(\pi), (184)

with λ=μ1\lambda=\mu_{1}. By the equivalence (183), we conclude that

‖S¯tΓ​F‖L2​(π¯Γ)2≤C​e−2​λ​t​‖F‖L2​(π¯Γ)2,t≥0,F∈L~02​(π¯Γ),\|\bar{S}^{\Gamma}_{t}F\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma})}\leq Ce^{-2\lambda t}\|F\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma})},\quad t\geq 0,\quad F\in\tilde{L}_{0}^{2}(\bar{\pi}_{\Gamma}), (185)

with C=c2c1C=\frac{c_{2}}{c_{1}}. Comparing (184) and (185), we see that the coupled process achieves the same exponential rate of convergence as the one-particles processes, but possibly with a worse constant CC in front of the exponential. The latter can be characterised in terms of the equivalence estimate (182).

Conclusively, the speed of convergence to equilibrium can be both faster (as in Example 70) and slower (as in Example 71) for coupled processes, in comparison with the underlying one-particle processes. We leave a more thorough investigation of the Poincaré inequality (170) for future work.

7 Outlook and future work

In this paper we have introduced a general framework for the construction and analysis of coupled MCMC samplers. Formulating the results in an abstract setting has allowed us to address both (possibly degenerate) diffusion processes as well as piecewise deterministic Markov processes, emphasising common structural properties. The analysis of appropriate central limit theorems has exposed notable connections to the theory of optimal transportation. We showed that the ensuing optimisation problem has singularity properties akin to those appearing in the usual Kantorovich formulation. We then studied a surrogate problem, leading to novel coupling strategies that seem promising for applications. Finally, we derived a functional inequality of Poincaré type suitable for the study of the exponential convergence to equilibrium for coupled processes.

Our work can be extended in several directions. On the theoretical side, proving or disproving the Conjectures 11, 17 and 19 would further illuminate the structural properties of the developed theory. Moreover, establishing a more rigorous connection between the optimal transport problems 1 and 2 with the usual Kantorovich formulation might lead to further developments bridging the theories of Markov processes and optimal transportation.

In terms of applications in sampling, a more detailed study of the couplings between many particles is needed, a starting point being the results in Section 5.2. Furthermore, it would be desirable to relax our assumption that the laws of the marginal processes remain unchanged, as this would allow for more pronounced interactions between the particles. In this regard, the inclusion of the methodology put forward in [52] in our framework would be of particular interest for practitioners.

In the broader context of statistical computation, it seems that coupling approaches along the lines developed here could be fruitfully applied in the context of the calculation of transport coefficients and sensitivities [5, 39]. More speculatively, it would be interesting to investigate the use of our ideas in the context of multilevel Monte Carlo [36] or computational optimal transport [69]. We leave these directions for future investigations.

Appendix A Random orthogonal transformations of Brownian motions

The following lemma has been extracted from [29, page 56], see also [66, Theorem 8.4.2]. This result states that the set of Brownian motions is preserved under possibly time-dependent linear transformations possessing certain orthogonality properties. Importantly, no regularity constraints with regard to the time-dependence are required beyond measurability. This fact is crucial in the proofs of Lemmas 22 and 27.

Lemma 72 (Random orthogonal transformations).

Suppose that the ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N}-valued stochastic process (Xt)t≥0(X_{t})_{t\geq 0} is a solution to the SDE

d​Xt=Ot​d​Wt,X0=x0,\mathrm{d}X_{t}=O_{t}\mathrm{d}W_{t},\quad X_{0}=x_{0}, (186)

where (Wt)t≥0(W_{t})_{t\geq 0} is an MM-dimensional standard Brownian motion generating the filtration (ℱt)t≥0(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t\geq 0}, and (Ot)t≥0(O_{t})_{t\geq 0} is a product-measurable (ℱt)t≥0(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t\geq 0}-adapted process taking values in ℝN×M\mathbb{R}^{N\times M}. Assume furthermore that

Ot​OtT=IN×NO_{t}O_{t}^{T}=I_{N\times N} (187)

for all t≥0t\geq 0, almost surely. Then (Xt)t≥0(X_{t})_{t\geq 0} is an NN-dimensional standard Brownian motion.

∫−∞0f⁡(s)​e−V⁡(s)​𝑑s+∫0∞f⁡(s)​e−V⁡(s)​𝑑s=0.\int_{-\infty}^{0}f(s)e^{-V(s)}\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{\infty}f(s)e^{-V(s)}\mathrm{d}s=0. (204)

Furthermore, the symmetry properties of ff and VV show that

∫−∞0f⁡(s)​e−V⁡(s)​𝑑s−∫0∞f⁡(s)​e−V⁡(s)​𝑑s=0,\int_{-\infty}^{0}f(s)e^{-V(s)}\mathrm{d}s-\int_{0}^{\infty}f(s)e^{-V(s)}\mathrm{d}s=0, (205)

using the substitution s↦−ss\mapsto-s. Equations (204) and (205) together imply that Φ⁡(0)=0\Phi(0)=0, for Φ\Phi as defined in (203). The claim now follows using an analogous argument to the one used in the proof of 1.). ∎

Proof of Lemma 61.

Recall from (135) that

δ​σF2​(Γα)=∫E¯ξ​d​π¯0,\delta\sigma_{F}^{2}(\Gamma_{\alpha})=\int_{\bar{E}}\xi\,\mathrm{d}\bar{\pi}_{0}, (206)

where ξ⁡(x,y)=ϕ⁡(x)​ϕ​(y)\xi(x,y)=\phi(x)\phi(y) and ϕ:ℝ×{−1,+1}→ℝ\phi:\mathbb{R}\times\{-1,+1\}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is the solution to the (one-particle) Poisson equation

θ​∂xϕ⁡(x,θ)+λ⁡(x,θ)​(ϕ⁡(x,−θ)−ϕ⁡(x,θ))=f⁡(x),π⁡(ϕ)=0.\theta\partial_{x}\phi(x,\theta)+\lambda(x,\theta)\left(\phi(x,-\theta)-\phi(x,\theta)\right)=f(x),\quad\pi(\phi)=0. (207)

Note that for convenience, we have assumed without loss of generality that π~​(f)=0\tilde{\pi}(f)=0. Let us now calculate

−ϕ(x,−θx)ϕ(y,θy)+ϕ(x,−θx)ϕ(y,−θy)])e−(V⁡(x)+V⁡(y))dxdy\displaystyle-\phi(x,-\theta_{x})\phi(y,\theta_{y})+\phi(x,-\theta_{x})\phi(y,-\theta_{y})\bigg]\Bigg)e^{-\left(V(x)+V(y)\right)}\,\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}y
=14∫ℝ2([α+⁣+(x,y)+α−⁣−(x,y)−α+⁣−(x,y)−α−⁣+(x,y)]⋅\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}\int_{{\mathbb{R}^{2}}}\Bigg(\bigg[\alpha_{++}(x,y)+\alpha_{--}(x,y)-\alpha_{+-}(x,y)-\alpha_{-+}(x,y)\bigg]\cdot
⋅[ϕ+(x)ϕ+(y)+ϕ−(x)ϕ−(y)−ϕ+(x)ϕ−(y)−ϕ−(x)ϕ+(y)])e−(V⁡(x)+V⁡(y))dxdy\displaystyle\cdot\bigg[\phi_{+}(x)\phi_{+}(y)+\phi_{-}(x)\phi_{-}(y)-\phi_{+}(x)\phi_{-}(y)-\phi_{-}(x)\phi_{+}(y)\bigg]\Bigg)e^{-\left(V(x)+V(y)\right)}\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}y
=14∫ℝ2([α+⁣+(x,y)+α−⁣−(x,y)−α+⁣−(x,y)−α−⁣+(x,y)]⋅\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}\int_{{\mathbb{R}^{2}}}\Bigg(\bigg[\alpha_{++}(x,y)+\alpha_{--}(x,y)-\alpha_{+-}(x,y)-\alpha_{-+}(x,y)\bigg]\cdot
